articles.title: Okinawa Voted for a New Governor
articles.full_text:
Koja Genta didn’t win because of his stance on U.S. bases. He won because of his vision for the economy.
Koja Genta greets a supporter as he celebrates his victory in the Okinawa governor’s election, Sep. 13, 2026.
On September 13, Japan’s Okinawa Prefecture held its gubernatorial election. Koja Genta, a 42-year-old former mayor of Naha City, emerged with a convincing victory – 59 percent (423,124 votes) to 38 percent (276,060 votes) – against incumbent Governor Denny Tamaki.
His election can create genuine – and long overdue – momentum to transform the relationship between the Japanese government and Okinawa from the confrontation over U.S. bases in the prefecture into a partnership to move Okinawa forward.
As a home to the U.S. Marines Third Expeditionary Force (III MEF) headquarters, local elections in Okinawa from the governor’s race on down always attract not only national attention but also a great deal of interest from the U.S. defense establishment. With the ongoing plan to realign and consolidate the U.S. Marine Corps’ presence in Okinawa, Sunday’s election was particularly critical.  
As a governor, Koja has a profile that is different from any of his predecessors. First and foremost, at the age of 42, he is the youngest governor that Okinawa has ever elected.  Born in 1983, he is also the first governor who was born after Okinawa reverted to Japan in 1972.
Furthermore, while he was born and grew up in Okinawa, he spent his formative years as a young adult in Tokyo as a college student, a civil servant at the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, and a program manager in the private sector.  
His profile – born and grew up in Okinawa but left his hometown for mainland Japan for higher education and employment before returning to Okinawa to run for office – crystallizes the economic challenge that the working-age generation in Okinawa has long been facing. Okinawa’s economy lacks diversity; it is heavily dependent on tourism. This makes employment in the prefecture more seasonal and temporary in nature. Furthermore, while its aging population continues to create greater demand for workers in senior living management, medical assistants, and nursing, there are far fewer opportunities for high-skilled and well-paying jobs. 
The local economy makes it challenging for the working-age population, especially younger people, to live in Okinawa and raise families. Its unemployment rate is twice as high as the national average, with persistent structural unemployment.       
Mindful of this reality, Koja placed vitalization of the Okinawan economy front and center in his election campaign.  His landslide victory – he earned the most votes in 40 out of 41 localities in Okinawa – demonstrates that Koja’s message of moving the Okinawan economy forward resonated much more than Tamaki’s message, which attempted to campaign by continuing to tap anti-base sentiment within the prefecture.
This election exposed a clear generational divide. The exit polls showed that over 60 percent of voters younger than 60 years old voted for Koja, while Tamaki continued to retain strong support among older constituents. That said, this split should not be reduced to a simplistic contest between “younger” vs. “older” Okinawans, let alone the stereotypical explanation of the younger generation being “pro-base” because they see a greater threat from China while the older generation remains “anti-base” due to their memories of the Battle of Okinawa and its tragic ending.  
Kaja’s victory reflects a much deeper shift in priorities among Okinawans. For many voters in their working and family-raising years, kitchen-table issues – such as stagnant incomes, inflation, lack of well-paying employment and the island’s overall economic prospects – have become much more urgent than repeating political battles over U.S. bases. Those long-running political fights have produced little practical change, let alone improvement in the local economy.  Exit polls clearly demonstrated this unmistakable shift, with a greater percentage of the voters identifying “economic growth” as their top issue of concern.  
Still, Koja’s position on relocating Marine Corps Air Station Futenma to Henoko – as agreed to by the U.S. and Japanese governments back in 1996 –  is significant. Koja argued that his acceptance of the existing relocation plan is not an endorsement of Okinawa’s disproportionate base burden. Rather, he insisted that the fastest, most practical way to eliminate the risk posed by Futenma is to work with the government to ensure the completion of the relocation. 
Koja ran on a practical platform of a three-pronged approach: complete the relocation to Henoko, demand that Tokyo establish a credible return date for the land currently occupied by Futenma and additional land south of Kadena Air Force Base, and begin planning for how to utilize the property upon return.  
What comes next should be the center of the new administration’s agenda. The eventual return of Futenma and other U.S. facilities south of Kadena Air Base presents Okinawa with a rare development opportunity. Land-use decisions, transportation links, housing, education, research, tourism, and private investment cannot be improvised after the fences come down. Koja should convene municipalities, residents, businesses, universities, and the national government to produce a transparent redevelopment strategy with timelines, financing, and measurable benefits for local communities. If managed well, base consolidation can become not merely a security adjustment but a catalyst for higher productivity and durable growth.
With Koja’s election, Okinawa will have a governor who has the backing not only from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and its coalition partner Nippon Ishin no Kai (the Japan Innovation Party) but also from other conservative and center-right political parties that endorsed Koja during the election. This allows the Takaichi government to attempt a “reset” of Tokyo’s relationship with Naha under Governor Koja as a partner.      
However, as tempting as it may be for the Japanese government to intensify its push toward completing the long-stalled Futenma relocation, Tokyo must first understand the drivers behind Koja’s decisive victory.  In other words, Tokyo needs to appreciate the reality that Koja’s convincing victory reflects more than a change of administration. It is a reflection of a strong public demand for a new direction for Okinawa, especially in its economy. 
Koja’s landslide is therefore not a blank check. It is a mandate for results: reduce the danger at Futenma, complete the relocation without further unnecessary delay, return the land on a dependable schedule, and convert that land into opportunity for Okinawans. The voters have chosen a younger leader who promised to move forward. His success will depend on whether every party to the agreement now does the same.

articles.title: From Nomad Festival to National Showcase: Kyrgyzstan Takes Center Stage
articles.full_text:
In early September, Kyrgyzstan hosted both the World Nomad Games and the SCO summit in a carefully choreographed spectacle of national power and pride.
The ethno-village of yurts in Kyrchyn gorge during the games. Sept. 3, 2026
In early September, the World Nomad Games returned to Kyrgyzstan for the first time in eight years. That same week, a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit was hosted in Bishkek. The capital went quiet.
Main roads were sealed off for motorcades. Shopping centers along the official routes closed. Residents were told, early and in public: if you can get out of town, get out. By September 1, traffic maps showed more than eighty restrictions. The streets were almost empty.
A few hours east, Kyrchyn gorge came alive. Yurts covered the meadow. Clay forts — built to recall the ancient Silk Road era — rose over the grass. Organizers said 150,000 people came through on day one. Visitors argued over bus seats. Private cars were turned away. 
Bishkek was told to clear out and shut down. The summer pasture was told to put on a show.
Eight years ago, when the games were last held beside Issyk-kul, the barricades and the spectacle were centered there. This time the games opened in the new Bishkek Arena, a 51,000-seat stadium, on the same weekend as the SCO summit. In the stands: Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Türkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
At the opening, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said: “Our foundation is independence, and our roots are in nomadic civilization. Our course is international friendship and partnership, and our future lies in building a developed, strong new Kyrgyzstan.”
He also announced that Kazan, in Russia’s Tatarstan, would host the next games in 2028. Moscow had sent a formal request, he said, and he thanked Putin.
Security around the opening ceremony was tight. Snipers stood on the arena roof. A three-kilometer radius was closed for the day. Japarov walked onstage as more than the host of a festival; he was a leader confident in the power he’s consolidated around himself. 
In February 2026, Japarov dismissed his longtime ally, then-head of the State Committee for National Security Kamchybek Tashiev, breaking a tandem that had ruled Kyrgyzstan since 2020. In January 2027, he’ll run for president again. 
The games were still about horses, yurts, and Kok Boru. The narrative frame around them is not. This was no longer a carnival by the lake, it was a state showcase.
Closer to the SCO summit, the main roads from the airport and through the center of the capital were shut down. Public transport was rerouted. Big malls and markets closed. On September 1, Bishkek really did empty out. Traffic cameras showed almost nothing moving.
Anyone still on the main streets when the motorcades passed by was taken out of the shot. Pedestrians were told to duck onto side streets. If they were already in the roadway, they were sent down into the underpasses. Tourists who had come for the games stood underground alongside locals and tried to work out what was happening.
“I don’t understand why they treat their own people like this,” a tourist from Germany said. “Why are they hiding them?” She sounded more confused than angry.
Kyrchyn was very far from the silenced capital. Yurts covered the meadow. Fortress walls and towers rose above them — not two props at the gate, but the whole outline of a town. Each of Kyrgyzstan’s seven regions, alongside Bishkek and Osh, had its own camp: its yurts, its food, its dancers. It rained. People danced anyway.
Getting to the gorge was a daunting challenge, one many took on. You could not drive in. There were not enough free buses. People waited more than an hour and argued over seats. Those who made it arrived at a crowded, wet, very loud festival. Foreign visitors filmed what they had come to film, and they looked just as happy as the locals. A Brazilian creator with some 300,000 followers said her Issyk-kul videos were “blowing up” at home. An Australian couple looked at the yurts in the mountain meadow and said, “This is exactly how we pictured it.” Social media — and not only in Kyrgyzstan — was filled with dancing in the rain and the opening-night spectacle. The opening ceremony’s dance caught on far beyond Kyrgyzstan. Users in neighboring countries filmed themselves repeating the choreography.
Since 2016, the World Nomad Games sporting program has almost doubled, from 23 sports to 43. Women have entered several of them. In Kyrgyz-style horseback archery this year, 45 women from 32 countries competed. On paper, that looks like a tradition opening up. On the ground, the archery field became one of the most crowded spots for journalists. Women in national dress, galloping, trying to hit a mark against not-so-distant snowy peaks, photographed beautifully. 
It was less beautiful up close. Kyrgyzstan’s women’s team was put together in two weeks. One coach ran both the men’s and women’s squads, but the focus stayed on the men. Equestrian sport is still treated as male territory in Kyrgyzstan. A woman, in the old traditions, is decoration — as are the girls in kyz kuumai, the bride-chase game.
“We ride no worse. We shoot no worse. Sometimes better,” said Aidana Usenbekova, 28, one of three Kyrgyz women on the horseback archery team. “All the horse sports are still seen as men’s sports. For the few girls who even get seen and make the national team, it’s twice as hard. We’re still fighting the stereotypes here. We didn’t even have time to prepare properly. We still put in a strong performance.”
Right before the start of the competition, their mounts were handed to other riders. 
“They told us those girls were guests, and we had to take whatever horses were left.” 
Aidana cried, then and there, out of sheer frustration at the perceived insult.
“That’s the attitude toward women in this sport. It’s contempt. It happened right before we went out. We all walked into the competition like that.”
The games needed the female archers. They look good in the frame: a woman on a horse, a bow, the mountains behind. 
On September 6, at the hippodrome in Cholpon-Ata, Kyrgyzstan beat Kazakhstan 12-0 in Kok Boru, then 7-2 in Kokpar the same day — the two games are similar but the former is Kyrgyzstan’s traditional version and the latter Kazakhstan’s. The stands roared. This was the spectacle the games were invented for. Fans had come from every region for that match. 
“I came for Manas,” said Tashtan, 75, who traveled from Uzgen for Kok Boru, referring to the legendary Kyrgyz hero. “I’m a big fan of his.”
There was a mess with tickets. More were sold than there were seats — fraud, people said. Japarov stepped in and ordered the gates be opened to anyone who wanted in. People who had bought tickets and waited in the crowd for the final never made it into the stadium.
Political analyst Temur Umarov doubts the leaders’ schedules were ever fully in Japarov’s hands. But the dates for the games and the SCO summit luckily lined up. Japarov used the week, Umarov says, to show Kyrgyz voters what he has long promised: order, a Kyrgyzstan visible in Central Asia on political par with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, something to be proud of. The show had two audiences. The main one was at home. 
“The core audience this was aimed at,” Umarov said, “was Kyrgyz citizens.”
articles.summary: In early September, Kyrgyzstan hosted both the World Nomad Games and the SCO summit in a carefully choreographed spectacle of national power and pride.

articles.title: What Has AUKUS Pillar II Achieved Over 5 Years?
articles.full_text:
Pillar II’s progress has proven difficult to judge – not due to a lack of activity, but because there’s no agreed metric for what success should look like.
It’s been five years since the leaders of Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States announced AUKUS, a security partnership designed to deepen technology and capability-sharing among the three countries.
While its much-publicized Pillar I component – centered on Australia’s acquisition of conventionally-armed, nuclear-powered submarines – is reported to be “on track,” the lesser-known Pillar II component has come under mounting criticism for “failing” to deliver fast enough.
As a framework for the joint development and fielding of advanced military capabilities, Pillar II was initially pegged by some analysts to be the “more consequential” arm of the AUKUS partnership – not only for delivering on a shorter timeline than Pillar I, but also for leveraging the latest technologies known to be reshaping how modern conflicts are fought.
In the years that have passed since its announcement, Pillar II’s progress has proven difficult to judge – not due to a lack of activity, but because there’s no agreed metric for what success should look like. For some, its incrementalism is indicative of its failure, while to others, the breadth of its objectives warrants a slow and steady approach. 
Five years on, it’s time to take stock of Pillar II’s objectives and efforts to better understand this evolving debate, and consider what lies ahead.  
Pillar II, known as Advanced Capabilities, involves the collaborative development, fielding and production of advanced military capabilities in six key areas: artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomy, cyber, electronic warfare, hypersonics and counter-hypersonics, quantum, and undersea warfare.
Developments in each of these technology areas are reshaping how conflicts are fought. The wars in Ukraine and Iran reveal how AI, unmanned systems, hypersonics, cyber, and electronic warfare have been leveraged in new ways by actors on all sides of these conflicts. 
It’s also no coincidence that these are technology areas where China is reported to be outperforming the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia in research and innovation. China is leading in 69 of 74 technologies deemed critical to strategic competition by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. AUKUS Pillar II is intended to close this gap by combining each country’s strengths in innovation, technology, and industry to create advanced military capabilities at a faster speed than any one of them could achieve individually. 
More specifically, the three AUKUS partners seek to achieve greater interoperability and industrial integration between participating countries. Part of this is achieved through co-developing new capabilities that are designed, from the outset, to integrate into each countries’ existing military platforms and processes. Similarly, significant changes to the policy landscape – or “enabling environment” – in each country intend to make it easier for them to share information and technology with each other.
It’s due to these reasons that some analysts believe Pillar II will generate “greater long-term value” than the Pillar I nuclear-powered submarines – not just for the advanced capabilities Pillar II would produce, but because of its long-term role in reducing barriers to collaboration between the three countries. 
Over the last five years, cooperation has taken place across the different workstreams. The most notable activities have primarily focused on the collaborative research, development, and testing of capabilities, and the achievement of regulatory alignment between AUKUS countries. One early example of this collaboration is a jointly developed AI algorithm for reconnaissance aircraft that was unveiled in December 2023 and used operationally in August 2025.
The table below summarizes the publicly reported Pillar II activities to date. 
Since the announcement of Pillar II wasn’t accompanied by a signature project, like the nuclear-powered submarines for Pillar I, judging the extent to which these activities count as progress depends on how success is measured. 
AUKUS countries have established defense trade exemptions for around 80 percent of U.S. defense exports to Australia and the U.K. that were previously subject to the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR). Experts agree that the regulatory reforms are necessary to facilitate technology and industrial collaboration between the three countries. 
That said, some argue that too much emphasis has been placed on these reforms as evidence that things are on track – especially since they haven’t completely resolved the issues created by tough U.S. defense export controls. If Pillar II’s success is measured against the delivery of an operational capability, the picture looks different. The testing and demonstration of new technologies, while evidence of successful collaboration, have not fulfilled Pillar II’s intention to deliver capability.
Others contend that Pillar II should be seen as more of a crawl-walk-run process. In this view, regulatory alignment and capability testing are legitimate outputs in their own right, since they have established the groundwork needed before genuine trilateral collaboration can happen. 
These contrasting metrics speak to a broader PR problem that has long plagued Pillar II. Since it was initially framed as a way of delivering a tangible product faster than Pillar I, the expectation of an AUKUS-branded output has loomed over Pillar II.  
Hence the most recent milestone: the announcement of the first Pillar II signature project in May 2026, which would see AUKUS countries jointly produce shared payloads and systems for uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs) by 2027. This comes after years of analysts calling for a signature project to demonstrate proof of concept and for Pillar II’s priorities to be narrowed. 
On paper, the logic is evident– the delivery of a UUV capability aligns with Pillar I’s focus on undersea warfare and complements surface vessel maritime operations. It also fulfils a stop-gap maritime capability for each country. Australia is expecting its first Virginia-class submarine from the United States in 2032. The U.S. is working to increase its submarine production from the current rate of 1.2-1.3 boats per year to 2.33 per year. The United Kingdom is focused  on the  sustainment of its Astute-class fleet, which are all currently in maintenance. 
Moving forward, Pillar II has several enduring structural challenges to overcome if it is to translate its ambitions into tangible capabilities. 
First, as of September 2026, roughly 20 percent of intra-AUKUS defense trade was not captured by licensing exemptions – and these sectors are directly relevant to Pillar II capability requirements. This includes technology areas like undersea acoustics, missile technology controlled under the Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR), and sensitive technical data and source code associated with advanced weapons and fire-control systems. Addressing this will require mitigating U.S. concerns about protecting sensitive technologies, maintaining competition within the U.S. defense industrial base, complying with domestic and international non-proliferation obligations, and preventing the compromise of critical technologies by strategic competitors. 
Second, unlike Pillar I, which has clear national funding architectures centered on the acquisition and construction of SSNs, Pillar II spans a much broader set of technologies and workstreams that cut across existing national capability programs. As a result, Pillar II lines of effort have had to pull resources from existing national capability priorities. This does not necessarily require AUKUS members to establish dedicated funding streams to realize Pillar II’s potential. But the three countries must ensure that they can reliably access the resources needed to deliver Pillar II technologies, even as they compete with other national defense priorities across their broader defense industrial ecosystems.
Third, AUKUS policymakers face the question of whether Pillar II should narrow its technological scope to enable more targeted funding, senior-level attention, and industrial capacity. Doing so would involve concentrating resources toward operational requirements, including long-range strike and targeting, multidomain missile defense, command, and control, and enhanced logistical networks. 
The U.K. Parliament’s Defense Committee concluded in its April 2026 AUKUS report that the breadth of Pillar II had become an impediment to delivery. This sentiment has also been reflected by the Pentagon’s scaling back in late 2025 of its initial list of 14 critical technologies – expected by the Joe Biden administration to maintain the U.S. military’s future superiority – to six: applied AI, biomanufacturing, contested logistics technologies, quantum and battlefield information dominance, scaled directed energy, and scaled hypersonics. AUKUS leaders are yet to offer clarity as to whether Pillar II is formally defining its future collaboration against operational challenges rather than its original technology categories.

articles.title: The Perils of Mind-Reading in the Taiwan Strait
articles.full_text:
Without sustained dialogue over Taiwan, Beijing and Washington are both vulnerable to dangerous misreadings of each other’s intentions.
The U.S. Navy Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Chung-Hoon observed PLAN Luyang III DDG 132 execute maneuvers in what the U.S. called “an unsafe manner” while the Chung-Hoon conducted a routine Taiwan Strait transit alongside the Halifax-class frigate HMCS Montreal, June 3, 2023.
Less than two weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s high-stakes visit to Washington, Beijing reportedly threatened to cancel the planned summit with U.S. President Donald Trump if the United States approved further arms sales to Taiwan. Despite the White House’s silence on arms sales, its top envoy to Taipei last week called securing peace in the Taiwan Strait “one of its top priorities” for the United States.
Beneath this routine exchange of rhetoric lies a persistent problem: For all the attention Beijing and Washington devote to Taiwan, sustained communication over the issue remains thin. With both sides heralding their own version of strategic ambiguity, much of what passes for communication instead takes place at arm’s length – through public statements, arms sales, military deployments, and exercises. Consequently, strategic mind-reading has become a routine part of the relationship.
But constant guessing can harden assumptions more than sharpen judgment, creating precisely the kind of miscalculation that pushes a crisis toward conflict. For all their differences, neither Beijing nor Washington is immune to the risk.
Beijing would seem to have an advantage in the mind-reading game. Unlike China, the United States exposes much of its internal friction in public: issues like defense spending, weapons stocks, and industrial buildout are openly debated and scrutinized. Washington’s apparent difficulty in mobilizing resources and coordinating allied efforts over Ukraine and Iran, set against increasingly fractured domestic politics, can easily be read as evidence of American power in decline. 
That perception has likely fed into Beijing’s calculations over Taiwan, where one of the hardest questions is not whether the United States has the capability to intervene, but whether it would do so quickly enough to shape the course of a crisis. Chinese strategists may therefore be tempted to treat signs of American political dysfunction and mobilization delays as evidence against timely U.S. intervention. Already, China’s leading government advisers have highlighted the practical obstacles to timely U.S. intervention, from defense-production bottlenecks exposed by the war in Ukraine to Washington’s reliance on allied bases and logistical support.
But precedent shows such readings can be dangerously incomplete. During the 1995-96 Taiwan Strait crisis, Beijing reportedly interpreted Washington’s restrained response to earlier Chinese military exercises as evidence that the United States would limit itself to diplomatic protest. Instead, as tensions escalated, the Clinton administration sharply raised the stakes by deploying two carrier battle groups toward Taiwan, reportedly catching Beijing by surprise.
Those in Beijing who doubt Washington’s willingness to intervene may take further confidence from China’s growing military advantages close to home. But the broader warning still applies: familiar patterns of American restraint can become unreliable guides once a crisis changes the political stakes. If Beijing mistakes visible constraints on American power for a reliable forecast of U.S. behavior over Taiwan, it could overestimate how much room remains for coercion before provoking an unexpected response.
Information asymmetry leaves Washington at least as dependent on mind-reading. The search for a Chinese “timeline” on seizing Taiwan has become something of a cottage industry. Some assessments have focused on 2027, when Xi has instructed the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) to meet important modernization goals; others now look to Taiwan’s 2028 election cycle; still others have inferred a much longer horizon from Beijing’s linkage of unification with “national rejuvenation,” a goal associated with 2049. The proliferation of competing dates reveals how uncertain outsiders are about the logic that actually drives Beijing’s decisions on Taiwan.
That uncertainty naturally pushes Washington toward what it can observe. Chinese military activity around Taiwan offers an obvious proxy: the frequency and scale of drills and patrols are all being scrutinized for clues about Beijing’s intentions. Yet those signals are becoming harder, not easier, to interpret as China normalizes a higher tempo of military activity around the island. The same exercise can function at once as coercive signaling, contingency preparation, and rehearsal for operations Beijing may – or may not – someday choose to execute.
The result is an uncomfortable ambiguity. More intensive PLA activity does not necessarily signal a decision to use force, while routine activity may mask a meaningful change in intent. As once exceptional behavior becomes normalized, Washington risks misreading signals in both directions: seeing imminent action where there is only coercion, or dismissing a real shift in Beijing’s intentions as just another exercise.
The greater danger is that these two forms of misreading can reinforce each other in a crisis. If Beijing expects Washington to respond slowly, it may push coercion further in the belief that there is still room to maneuver. Washington, seeing a sharper escalation than expected, may interpret it as evidence that Beijing has already crossed a political threshold and respond more forcefully. That response, in turn, could convince Beijing that U.S. intervention is becoming imminent, narrowing the space for restraint on both sides.
The next crisis would leave little time to sort signal from intent. That is why sustained political and military communication – now beginning to regain momentum amid renewed high-level engagement between Xi and Trump – should be pursued even in the absence of deeper strategic trust, if only to strengthen deterrence and reduce the risk of miscalculation. Regular contact gives both sides a chance to explain what particular actions are meant to convey, learn how those actions are being received, and correct dangerous interpretations before they begin shaping the next move.
Beijing and Washington will continue to watch each other closely across the Taiwan Strait. They should also leave themselves a way to ask what they are actually seeing.
Less than two weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s high-stakes visit to Washington, Beijing reportedly threatened to cancel the planned summit with U.S. President Donald Trump if the United States approved further arms sales to Taiwan. Despite the White House’s silence on arms sales, its top envoy to Taipei last week called securing peace in the Taiwan Strait “one of its top priorities” for the United States.
Beneath this routine exchange of rhetoric lies a persistent problem: For all the attention Beijing and Washington devote to Taiwan, sustained communication over the issue remains thin. With both sides heralding their own version of strategic ambiguity, much of what passes for communication instead takes place at arm’s length – through public statements, arms sales, military deployments, and exercises. Consequently, strategic mind-reading has become a routine part of the relationship.
But constant guessing can harden assumptions more than sharpen judgment, creating precisely the kind of miscalculation that pushes a crisis toward conflict. For all their differences, neither Beijing nor Washington is immune to the risk.
Beijing would seem to have an advantage in the mind-reading game. Unlike China, the United States exposes much of its internal friction in public: issues like defense spending, weapons stocks, and industrial buildout are openly debated and scrutinized. Washington’s apparent difficulty in mobilizing resources and coordinating allied efforts over Ukraine and Iran, set against increasingly fractured domestic politics, can easily be read as evidence of American power in decline. 
That perception has likely fed into Beijing’s calculations over Taiwan, where one of the hardest questions is not whether the United States has the capability to intervene, but whether it would do so quickly enough to shape the course of a crisis. Chinese strategists may therefore be tempted to treat signs of American political dysfunction and mobilization delays as evidence against timely U.S. intervention. Already, China’s leading government advisers have highlighted the practical obstacles to timely U.S. intervention, from defense-production bottlenecks exposed by the war in Ukraine to Washington’s reliance on allied bases and logistical support.
But precedent shows such readings can be dangerously incomplete. During the 1995-96 Taiwan Strait crisis, Beijing reportedly interpreted Washington’s restrained response to earlier Chinese military exercises as evidence that the United States would limit itself to diplomatic protest. Instead, as tensions escalated, the Clinton administration sharply raised the stakes by deploying two carrier battle groups toward Taiwan, reportedly catching Beijing by surprise.
Those in Beijing who doubt Washington’s willingness to intervene may take further confidence from China’s growing military advantages close to home. But the broader warning still applies: familiar patterns of American restraint can become unreliable guides once a crisis changes the political stakes. If Beijing mistakes visible constraints on American power for a reliable forecast of U.S. behavior over Taiwan, it could overestimate how much room remains for coercion before provoking an unexpected response.
Information asymmetry leaves Washington at least as dependent on mind-reading. The search for a Chinese “timeline” on seizing Taiwan has become something of a cottage industry. Some assessments have focused on 2027, when Xi has instructed the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) to meet important modernization goals; others now look to Taiwan’s 2028 election cycle; still others have inferred a much longer horizon from Beijing’s linkage of unification with “national rejuvenation,” a goal associated with 2049. The proliferation of competing dates reveals how uncertain outsiders are about the logic that actually drives Beijing’s decisions on Taiwan.
That uncertainty naturally pushes Washington toward what it can observe. Chinese military activity around Taiwan offers an obvious proxy: the frequency and scale of drills and patrols are all being scrutinized for clues about Beijing’s intentions. Yet those signals are becoming harder, not easier, to interpret as China normalizes a higher tempo of military activity around the island. The same exercise can function at once as coercive signaling, contingency preparation, and rehearsal for operations Beijing may – or may not – someday choose to execute.
The result is an uncomfortable ambiguity. More intensive PLA activity does not necessarily signal a decision to use force, while routine activity may mask a meaningful change in intent. As once exceptional behavior becomes normalized, Washington risks misreading signals in both directions: seeing imminent action where there is only coercion, or dismissing a real shift in Beijing’s intentions as just another exercise.
The greater danger is that these two forms of misreading can reinforce each other in a crisis. If Beijing expects Washington to respond slowly, it may push coercion further in the belief that there is still room to maneuver. Washington, seeing a sharper escalation than expected, may interpret it as evidence that Beijing has already crossed a political threshold and respond more forcefully. That response, in turn, could convince Beijing that U.S. intervention is becoming imminent, narrowing the space for restraint on both sides.
The next crisis would leave little time to sort signal from intent. That is why sustained political and military communication – now beginning to regain momentum amid renewed high-level engagement between Xi and Trump – should be pursued even in the absence of deeper strategic trust, if only to strengthen deterrence and reduce the risk of miscalculation. Regular contact gives both sides a chance to explain what particular actions are meant to convey, learn how those actions are being received, and correct dangerous interpretations before they begin shaping the next move.
Beijing and Washington will continue to watch each other closely across the Taiwan Strait. They should also leave themselves a way to ask what they are actually seeing.

Consequently, strategic mind-reading has become a routine part of the relationship.

articles.title: Japan Faces Hard Choices in Weaning off Russian Energy
articles.full_text:
Beyond the question of energy security, Tokyo may want to avoid antagonizing Russia further by cutting off LNG purchases.
The Prigorodnoye Production Complexof the Sakhalin-II LNG Project, located in Korsakov City District of Sakhalin Oblast, Russia.
Japan is one of the most energy-insecure countries in the world relative to the size of its population and economy. Liquified natural gas (LNG) accounts for 30 percent of its electricity generation, and Japan imports more than 97 percent of its total LNG. Japan’s supplies of crude oil and coal are almost 100 percent imported.
Successive energy shocks produced by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have raised household costs and depressed growth. The International Energy Agency forecast that Japanese electricity prices for the second half of 2026 will surge 40 percent year-on-year, compared to only 25 percent for the European Union. 
This context helps to explain why Japan has continued to resist pressure from the United States to phase out its procurement of Russian LNG from the Sakhalin-II project in the Russian Far East. The Takaichi government justifies its stance by asserting that Russian LNG plays an “extremely important role” in Japan’s energy security. 
Domestic gas industry leaders warn that efforts to substitute the 5 million tonnes of LNG Japan buys from Russia annually – amounting to 9 percent of its total LNG imports – would risk supply shortages and increased costs for consumers. Cargoes from Sakhalin Island reach Japan in only two or three days, resulting in significantly lower transport costs compared to the seven days for Australian LNG and 20-40 days from the U.S. Gulf Coast. As Japanese households strain under a continuing cost-of-living crunch, there is little political appetite in Tokyo for measures that could add to that pain.
This June, the U.S. Treasury extended Japan’s sanctions waiver for purchases of Russian LNG until the end of 2026, marking the fifth extension since restrictions were introduced in 2022. However, Tokyo’s lobbying for exemptions is unlikely to succeed indefinitely. Officials must plan for the possibility that sooner or later, patience in Washington will run out. 
Does the Takaichi administration have the stomach to make a major break with Russia? A litmus test came in August with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s unprecedented visit to one of the four disputed Kuril Islands controlled by Russia. Japan regards the islands as “illegally occupied” and the dispute remains the main reason both sides have never signed a formal treaty ending World War II. Given the importance of the issue to Japanese foreign policy, Putin’s incendiary move demanded a forceful reply.
Instead, Takaichi’s response – calling the visit “absolutely unacceptable” and saying it had “hurt the public sentiment of the Japanese people” – was panned domestically as weak and inadequate. The government announced it was weighing further economic sanctions and other countermeasures but has yet to follow through. According to government insiders, concerns over energy loomed large and any cessation of imports from Sakhalin-II was ruled out. 
Putin’s provocative visit underlined the failure of former Prime Minister Abe Shinzo’s strategy of stepping up engagement with Russia in the hopes of resolving the territorial dispute. This effort, too, has links to Japan’s energy policy. As part of the economic sweeteners Tokyo extended to Moscow, its companies invested in Russian energy and infrastructure, taking equity stakes in Sakhalin-I and -II. These efforts not only failed to pay off but that the needle has now swung sharply in the opposite direction. Rather than inducing positive behavior from Moscow, those Japanese investments created dependencies that constrain Tokyo’s actions.
Japan is not ready to wholly abandon this Abe-era strategy. However, its continuing energy purchases and the sending of business delegations to Moscow risk negatively impacting its reputational standing among G7 allies. Critics can point to the example of the EU, which was far more reliant on Russian energy than Japan but has moved to institute a complete ban on Russian gas imports by September 2027.
Looking ahead, Japan is faced with difficult choices as the bulk of its Sakhalin-II LNG contracts are due to expire between 2028 and 2033. Domestic buyers’ preference for long-term contracts to avoid spot market volatility limits options and requires extensive planning and supplier diplomacy in advance. Simultaneously, Japan will be competing with strong demand from other Asian customers, as the Iran-U.S. war has cut off most of Qatari LNG from the global market and put its liquefaction facilities out of commission for years.
Japan may look to buy more from Australia or the United States. However, Australian gas production is reaching a plateau, while U.S. LNG cargoes loaded in the Gulf of Mexico must either transit the Panama Canal, which is increasingly susceptible to drought-induced closures and fee rises, or take the long, expensive route around the Cape of Good Hope. 
Canada is emerging as a major LNG exporter, with significant capacity coming online between 2028–2032. Loaded on the Pacific Coast, Canadian LNG is cost-competitive and reaches Japan in a chokepoint-free journey taking only 10 days. 
However, none of these alternative supplies will be as cheap and accessible as buying LNG from Russia. The broader risk is that abandoning energy cooperation will torpedo bilateral relations and close the door to a diplomatic resolution of the disputed Kuril Islands. The costs of further antagonizing Russia, at a time when Japan faces simultaneous security challenges emanating from both China and North Korea, may simply be too high.

articles.title: A New Kind of Cold War? China-US Competition in Latin America
articles.full_text:
Trump returned to the presidency with renewed determination to mitigate Chinese influence worldwide, giving particular interest to the Western Hemisphere.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping pose for a photo at Zhongnanhai in Beijing, China, May 15, 2026.
Managing bilateral relations with China has long been a topic of intense discussion and debate among top U.S. officials. From the beginning of the 21st century until the mid-2010s, the dominant approach favored a policy of “shared responsibility” for handling international affairs. However, over the last decade, an approach of strategic competition or great power competition has prevailed, across the tenures of both Presidents Donald Trump (2017–2021 and 2025–2029) and Joe Biden (2021–2025).
Strategic competition is not new in the history of U.S. foreign policy, as it was the dominant approach during the Cold War. Back then, Washington considered it a matter of national security to exert control over those zones considered part of its sphere of influence and, at the same time, to expel the Soviet Union, its former enemy, from the same regions. 
Now, the United States believes that China’s growth has led Beijing to become a similar threat. Washington sees this threat in a variety of Chinese tactics, including the use of trade bullying practices, the deployment of advanced weapons, the theft of intellectual property, and last but not least, the strengthening of its control over economic zones and critical infrastructure, especially those which could be used for dual military and economic purposes. 
Trump returned to the presidency with renewed determination to mitigate Chinese influence worldwide, giving particular interest to the Western Hemisphere. The 2025 National Security Strategy (NSS) stated that China’s presence in Latin America and the Caribbean poses a challenge to U.S. hegemony not only in the region, but also around the world. The main arguments relate to Beijing’s control of raw materials in the region and its increasing participation in regional supply chains – sometimes flooding countries with its products – but also the elevated number of foreign direct investment transactions registered within the last decade, the building of several infrastructure projects, and financial cooperation with regional countries through loans-for-oil and, more recently, swap deals. 
U.S. concerns about China are not merely economic in scope, but political. If, before, the Chinese government acted as a diplomatic power whose engagement with Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) was not oriented publicly toward targeting third countries (a sly reference to the U.S.), China no longer hides its intentions to counterbalance U.S. power in the region. China now presents itself as the biggest and most relevant power from the Global South and one trying to integrate more regional countries into its sphere of influence. 
In the democratic arena, despite China’s pragmatic approach of maintaining relations with both left and right parties, its closeness with governments that have expressed anti-American rhetoric and its silence in condemning some actions that have eroded institutional democratic frameworks (i.e., Nicaragua, Venezuela, Bolivia, and Cuba) positions Beijing as, arguably, posing a fundamental threat to the maintenance of the liberal democratic model in the region. It is important to remark that during the past century, spreading this political model was one of the bases on which American power was cemented in the Western Hemisphere. 
For a variety of reasons – political, economic, military, and strategic – the United States desires a reduction in Chinese influence. To advance this goal, Washington has presented a strategy based on three main aspects: a revamped version of the Monroe Doctrine, the concept of Greater North America – which includes countries around the Caribbean Sea, and into the northern Atlantic to encompass Greenland, and Iceland – and the formation of a new security coalition called the Shield of the Americas. 
China and the U.S. are engaged in strategic competition primarily in the LAC. This region, which the U.S. considers part of its first ring of security, has seen significant economic engagement with China over that quarter-century. China is now the region’s second-largest trading partner, its biggest lender, and a major source of financing for hundreds of infrastructure projects.
The U.S. government has primarily focused on reducing or eliminating China’s involvement in these economic activities. The most notable action has been to oust CK Hutchison, a Hong Kong-based company, from managing the ports of Balboa and Cristóbal, on either side of the Panama Canal. Initially, the Trump administration pressured the Panamanian government to expel CK Hutchison from the country, citing certain clauses in the 1979 bilateral treaty that returned the canal to Panama. Subsequently, the BlackRock hedge fund attempted to purchase the rights from CK Hutchison, but the Chinese government refused. Finally, a Panamanian judge ruled against CK Hutchison, and the final decision is pending new demands at the international arbitration courts. 
Other ports of interest to the U.S. are located in Mexico, such as Manzanillo (Pacific) and Veracruz (Atlantic), both of which are partially managed by CK Hutchison. The Pacific Ocean port of Chancay in Peru, operated by Chinese shipping giant Cosco, has also been the subject of controversy. Peruvian courts have ruled that activities inside the port must be inspected by local authorities. The Chinese side appealed that decision, claiming that the port is private, but without success. Furthermore, the U.S. government has announced $1.5 billion in funding to modernize the Peruvian military base in El Callao, near Chancay Port. 
The regional oil industry is also a top priority sector in the U.S. competition with China. Currently, the Trump administration’s control over the Venezuelan oil industry has prevented China from being awarded new oil projects, particularly in the Orinoco Oil Belt (OOB), the world’s largest oil reserve. In Argentina, Washington has also put enough pressure on the government to ban Huawei from participating in fiber optic and connectivity projects around the Vaca Muerta oil deposits. 
Similar paths have been taken in the lithium industries of Bolivia and Mexico. After President Rodrigo Paz issued an edict, Bolivia ordered a halt to, and review of, contracts signed by his predecessor with China to exploit the lithium reservoirs in the Uyuni Salt Flat. Mexico, for its part, saw former President López Obrador withdraw the Bacanora project and nationalize its operations in 2022 to reduce potential conflicts with its northern neighbor. 
Another sensitive issue for Washington is the development of 5G networks. For example, the Panamanian government announced that it would dismantle 13 telecommunications towers operated by Huawei in 2025 and replace them with American technology. Meanwhile, the Chilean government stopped the implementation of a new transoceanic optical fiber cable connecting Chile to China after facing strong pressure from the U.S. government. A few years ago, the Biden administration pressured the former Costa Rican president not to grant Huawei a concession to develop the country’s 5G network.
Last but not least, the Trump administration has focused on mitigating Chinese influence in Mexico, its main trading partner, which is sensitive to U.S. national security and economic development. Since taking office again, Trump has urged President Claudia Sheinbaum to impose tariffs on Chinese auto parts, electric vehicles, shoes, home appliances, and textiles. The Trump administration has also focused on mitigating China’s reexporting practices in Mexico, a country that, according to the White House, has served as a backdoor to introduce Chinese products into the North American Free Trade Zone. 
To prevent distortion and ensure the fulfillment of its hemispheric policy, Washington has developed a new security alliance with 19 regional countries called the Shield of the Americas (SoA). In this initial phase, the alliance aims to reduce drug trafficking and attack organized criminal organizations. It will also provide American military assistance to allied countries that request it, in order to prevent internal destabilization.
However, given present realist U.S. foreign policy, it is likely that the SoA will soon focus on preventing any military incursions or deployments by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) in the region. From an American perspective, this is understandable when considering that one of the main U.S. concerns about China in the region is the potential dual use of critical infrastructure for military and economic purposes. 
These actions, which are part of an updated version of the Monroe Doctrine, send a clear message to the region. Latin American and Caribbean countries must decide whether to prioritize their economic, military, and political relations with the United States or China. If they choose the U.S., the country will integrate them into its sphere of influence. Conversely, if they adopt a pro-China approach, they could eventually face different kinds of economic, political, and military coercion. One thing seems clear: the U.S. is willing to use all aspects of its national power to reduce China’s presence in Latin America and the Caribbean. 
This approach has been generally well-received in the region. Most countries in the greater North American region, excluding Greenland, Canada, and Iceland, have adopted a hedging strategy in favor of the U.S., reducing their political contacts with Beijing in anticipation of a possible deterioration of their bilateral relationship with Washington.
Other countries with relevant economic ties to China, such as Ecuador, Chile, Argentina, and Peru, have presidents who are politically aligned with Washington, but they remain economically engaged with Beijing. This opens the possibility of developing a new triangular relationship between China, the U.S., and Latin America. This strategy seems to be a form of buffering.
Brazil, a global partner of China in the BRICS bloc, and anti-American dictatorships such as Nicaragua and Cuba have expressed their opposition to the current U.S. approach to foreign policy in the region. These countries are keeping their political and economic links with China and refusing any kind of collaboration with Washington. The U.S. is targeting this group, which has chosen a confrontational strategy, in an attempt to change their foreign policy stances.
Finally, there is a group of countries that, despite their relative importance in their respective subregions, act more like free riders – these include some Caribbean countries, as well as Paraguay, Uruguay, and Guatemala. They align with either China or the U.S. depending on changes in the political, economic, and military contexts. 
Although the U.S. rejects the idea that its current policy against China in the region is a 21st-century version of the Cold War, its realist approach focuses on national interests and securing the LAC as its primary zone of influence (or “backyard,” as some officials have called it). In practice, this means that the Trump administration is not hesitating to use coercive tools to secure its position and influence in the region. This includes considering the possibility of military action, as seen with Venezuela, and economic sanctions, such as against Cuba.
Conversely, China, which has also avoided direct confrontation with the U.S., recognizes that the current era demands robust responses to U.S. challenges to its presence in Latin America and the Caribbean. Until now, Beijing has employed two strategies simultaneously. The first is rhetorical and aims to show that Washington’s bullying tactics do not align with the rules-based international system or good diplomatic practice; rather, they resemble Cold War ideology. The second strategy is legal and attempts to counter the coercive measures taken against its companies in Latin America according to international law. Recently, to protect itself and reduce its vulnerability, China has signed various agreements on the reciprocal promotion and protection of investments with its partners in the LAC. 
Additionally, China is employing other strategies. The most relevant is strategic patience. Beijing believes that the current U.S. coercive measures and counterbalancing policies will expire in 2028 when Trump’s second term ends and that the U.S. government hasn’t established a long-term strategy. 
Whether U.S. policies remain on the current track beyond 2028, at present Washington is willing to continue to do whatever it takes to mitigate Chinese influence in the region. This means that Xi Jinping’s government will most likely face increased pressure in the region until at least 2028 and possibly beyond. 
Importantly, during the last Democratic administration, Biden also implemented a foreign policy aimed at reducing Chinese influence in the region. And there are currently bipartisan efforts in the U.S. to develop a long-term approach beyond 2028 to address the challenges posed by Chinese influence in the region.
Undoubtedly, this panorama puts China in a dilemma. It must decide whether to confront U.S. measures against its interests in the region with stronger, more powerful tools, including deeper cooperation with its regional allies. Or, it could act passively, waiting for the end of Trump’s administration – and risk misjudging the solidity of wider Washington’s sentiments about China. 
No matter what option China chooses, it seems almost certain that the U.S., led by Trump or any other future president, will continue to implement a strategy aimed at reducing Chinese influence in Latin America and the Caribbean for at least the next decade. Great power competition is here to stay. Ultimately, Beijing is realizing that its previously touted peaceful rise is presenting new challenges, at least in the LAC, the historic zone of American influence.
articles.summary: Trump returned to the presidency with renewed determination to mitigate Chinese influence worldwide, giving particular interest to the Western Hemisphere.

articles.title: JASDF Global Hawk Presumed to Have Crashed off Western Japan
articles.full_text:
The incident could strain Japan’s persistent wide-area surveillance capabilities, as the JASDF operates only three of the high-altitude unmanned aircraft.
A RQ-4B Global Hawk in service with the JASDF.
A Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) RQ-4B Global Hawk is presumed to have crashed into the Sea of Japan (East Sea) on September 15 after experiencing communication problems and disappearing from radar. It’s the first such incident involving a JASDF Global Hawk, a high-altitude, unmanned surveillance aircraft manufactured by U.S. defense firm Northrop Grumman.
The aircraft, assigned to the 502nd Squadron of the Airborne Warning and Control Wing at Misawa Air Base in Aomori Prefecture, took off from the base at around 10:20 a.m., according to the JASDF.
Problems connecting with the aircraft’s communications equipment began after 12:55 p.m. Three minutes later, at around 12:58 p.m., its radar track disappeared over waters about 50 kilometers north of Tottori Prefecture in western Japan.
Japan immediately mounted a search for the missing UAV. The effort involved two F-15J fighters, a U-125A search-and-rescue aircraft, a UH-60J helicopter, and a KC-46A tanker from the JASDF, as well as the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force frigate Agano and missile boat Hayabusa.
The Japan Coast Guard discovered floating debris at around 2:19 p.m., and a JASDF F-15J fighter reported a debris sighting six minutes later. The U-125A search-and-rescue aircraft photographed the debris at 3:12 p.m. By 5:20 p.m., the JASDF had determined from the photographs that the debris was likely from the missing Global Hawk.
“Based on the floating objects discovered, the aircraft is presumed to have crashed,” the Air Staff Office said in its second report on the incident.
The cause remains under investigation. No damage outside the Self-Defense Forces had been reported as of 5 p.m.
The incident raises questions not only about what caused the Global Hawk to go down but also about the potential impact on Japan’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities.
At a press conference earlier on September 15, JASDF Chief of Staff General Morita Takehiro said the aircraft “was not on a training flight,” but declined to disclose what it had been doing.
Asked by this author whether the Global Hawk was likely to have crashed, Morita said at the time that the JASDF was considering “all possibilities” as it conducted the search. The subsequent discovery of debris led the service to presume that the aircraft had indeed crashed.
The JASDF operates three RQ-4Bs, all based at Misawa. Morita said this was the first time a JASDF Global Hawk had gone missing.
Japan began acquiring the Global Hawk in fiscal year 2015 to strengthen its persistent wide-area surveillance capabilities. The first aircraft arrived at Misawa in March 2022; the third arrived in June 2023, completing the planned three-aircraft fleet.
The RQ-4B is one of the JASDF’s key intelligence-gathering platforms. With a wingspan of about 40 meters and a length of about 15 meters, the UAV can remain airborne for around 36 hours and operate at altitudes of around 60,000 feet. Its high-altitude endurance allows it to monitor vast areas for extended periods without putting an aircrew at risk.
It is also an expensive asset. Japanese Defense Ministry documents put the unit cost of a Global Hawk at approximately 17.3 billion yen ($111.7 million). If the aircraft is ultimately confirmed lost, it would represent not only a significant financial loss but also the loss of one-third of Japan’s small Global Hawk fleet.
Retired JASDF Lt. Gen. Araki Junichi told NHK that a simple loss of communications would not necessarily explain the presumed crash because the aircraft is programmed to return to base if communications are lost. He suggested that an engine or other mechanical problem may have prevented normal flight, although the cause has yet to be established.
Araki also warned that losing one of the three aircraft could make continuous surveillance operations more difficult, potentially requiring other aircraft to compensate and increasing the burden on operational units.
The immediate priority is to recover as much of the aircraft as possible and determine what happened during the critical three-minute period between the onset of communication problems and the disappearance of its radar track.
Investigators will also need to establish what the aircraft was doing at the time, why communications failed, whether its automatic return-to-base function was activated, and why the aircraft was apparently unable to continue flying or return to base.
The answers will be important not only for preventing a recurrence, but also for assessing the reliability of a strategically important surveillance capability at a time when Japan is seeking to strengthen persistent intelligence-gathering around its increasingly contested neighborhood.
A Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) RQ-4B Global Hawk is presumed to have crashed into the Sea of Japan (East Sea) on September 15 after experiencing communication problems and disappearing from radar. It’s the first such incident involving a JASDF Global Hawk, a high-altitude, unmanned surveillance aircraft manufactured by U.S. defense firm Northrop Grumman.
The aircraft, assigned to the 502nd Squadron of the Airborne Warning and Control Wing at Misawa Air Base in Aomori Prefecture, took off from the base at around 10:20 a.m., according to the JASDF.
Problems connecting with the aircraft’s communications equipment began after 12:55 p.m. Three minutes later, at around 12:58 p.m., its radar track disappeared over waters about 50 kilometers north of Tottori Prefecture in western Japan.
Japan immediately mounted a search for the missing UAV. The effort involved two F-15J fighters, a U-125A search-and-rescue aircraft, a UH-60J helicopter, and a KC-46A tanker from the JASDF, as well as the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force frigate Agano and missile boat Hayabusa.
The Japan Coast Guard discovered floating debris at around 2:19 p.m., and a JASDF F-15J fighter reported a debris sighting six minutes later. The U-125A search-and-rescue aircraft photographed the debris at 3:12 p.m. By 5:20 p.m., the JASDF had determined from the photographs that the debris was likely from the missing Global Hawk.
“Based on the floating objects discovered, the aircraft is presumed to have crashed,” the Air Staff Office said in its second report on the incident.
The cause remains under investigation. No damage outside the Self-Defense Forces had been reported as of 5 p.m.
The incident raises questions not only about what caused the Global Hawk to go down but also about the potential impact on Japan’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities.
At a press conference earlier on September 15, JASDF Chief of Staff General Morita Takehiro said the aircraft “was not on a training flight,” but declined to disclose what it had been doing.
articles.summary: The incident could strain Japan’s persistent wide-area surveillance capabilities, as the JASDF operates only three of the high-altitude unmanned aircraft.

articles.title: China and Mexico: How Far Should Technology Cooperation Go?
articles.full_text:
The Mexican government is deepening ties with Beijing in some of the sectors most sensitive to U.S. security concerns.
Rosaura Ruiz Gutiérrez, head of Mexico’s Secretariat of Science, Humanities, Technology, and Innovation (Secihti), shakes hands with Chinese Minister of Science and Technology Yin Hejun at the the Ninth Meeting of the Science and Technology Subcommittee of the Mexico-China Permanent Binational Commission, Sep. 6, 2026.
Between July and September 2026, scientific and technological cooperation between Mexico and China gained new momentum. Rosaura Ruiz Gutiérrez, head of Mexico’s Secretariat of Science, Humanities, Technology, and Innovation (Secihti), first met with Chinese Ambassador to Mexico Chen Daojiang and later co-chaired, alongside Chinese Minister of Science and Technology Yin Hejun, the Ninth Meeting of the Science and Technology Subcommittee of the Mexico-China Permanent Binational Commission. Since the mechanism was established in 2004, no Chinese minister of science and technology had personally participated in its meetings.
At the meeting, the two governments signed a memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation among universities, public institutions, and companies in research, digital infrastructure, advanced technology transfer, and public-private partnerships. The areas discussed included artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, robotics, electromobility, and semiconductors. Secihti has also acknowledged that it is exploring opportunities to work with Huawei on high-performance computing, AI, and specialized talent development.
These developments come at a particularly difficult moment in Mexico’s relationship with the United States, which is spilling over into China-Mexico relations. 
Since January, the Mexican government has imposed new tariffs on 1,463 product categories originating in countries with which Mexico has no free trade agreement. Although China is not the only country affected, it has borne much of the impact: between January and May, Chinese imports covered by these measures fell by 28.4 percent. In sectors such as footwear and passenger vehicles, the declines reached 59 percent and 35 percent, respectively.
Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard has defended these measures as a way to protect Mexican industry. Yet they are difficult to separate from Washington’s pressure over China’s economic presence in Mexico and the upcoming USMCA review. On this issue, Claudia Sheinbaum’s government appears to have chosen to partially accommodate Trump in order to preserve an economic relationship that is exceedingly difficult to replace.
At the same time, Mexico has sought closer political ties with China amid poor treatment from the United States. On September 4, U.S. President Donald Trump declared from the Oval Office that Mexico had “nothing that we really need,” beyond “spicy tamales, tomatoes, a couple of things.” 
Just three days later, Mexico’s Foreign Secretary Roberto Velasco traveled to Beijing to meet with Wang Yi. There, the Chinese foreign minister expressed support for Mexico against “foreign interference” and argued that China-Mexico relations “are not directed at any third party and should not be affected by any third party.” Neither government explicitly mentioned the United States, but both appeared to have it very much in mind.
There is nothing inherently problematic about Mexico seeking to diversify its international relations. If anything, the uncertainty created by Trump demonstrates the risks of depending excessively on a single partner. But if the Mexican government is trying to reduce commercial frictions with Washington, how should we interpret its simultaneous deepening of ties with Beijing in some of the sectors most sensitive to U.S. security concerns?
Recent exchanges between Secihti and its Chinese counterparts reveal at least three particularly problematic areas. The first concerns the technologies chosen for deeper cooperation. Artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and high-performance computing – all explicitly discussed during these meetings – are not ordinary industries. They are at the heart of the China-U.S. competition to achieve greater technological autonomy, control supply chains, and preserve industrial and military advantages. Washington has therefore spent much of the past decade restricting China’s access to advanced chips and other dual-use technologies.
The second concerns Huawei. Before the Subcommittee meeting, Secihti itself announced that it was exploring cooperation with the Chinese company in high-performance computing, AI, and specialized talent development. Since the first Trump administration, Huawei has been at the center of U.S. restrictions on Chinese technology over security and espionage concerns. These concerns have even generated tensions between Washington and allied governments over Chinese companies’ participation in 5G networks and other digital infrastructure.
Finally, Secihti’s exchanges with Chinese representatives have placed considerable emphasis on student and researcher mobility, as well as cooperation among universities, research centers, and companies. Promoting these exchanges is perfectly legitimate and can yield real benefits. Yet when academic cooperation overlaps with dual-use technologies, it requires safeguards different from those of conventional academic exchange. The U.S. Congress has warned about ties between certain Chinese universities and scientific programs and Beijing’s “military-civil fusion” strategy, through which advances developed in civilian settings can contribute to military capabilities.
This does not make every Chinese student or researcher a security risk – a conclusion that would be both unfair and absurd. But it does require distinguishing between cooperation on agricultural pests – as the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) and the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences already do – and transferring knowledge related to semiconductors, AI, or high-performance computing. Precisely because Secihti’s new agenda encompasses both kinds of cooperation, Mexico should be able to tell the difference.
It is possible, of course, that many of these agreements will never reach the scale suggested by official statements. Latin America’s experience shows that many memorandums signed with China produce more declarations and photo opportunities than lasting projects. Even so, it is striking that the priorities discussed in Secihti’s exchanges closely resemble sectors promoted by Beijing’s industrial policy over the past decade, from Made in China 2025 to its policy documents on Latin America and the Caribbean.
Diversifying Without Creating New Dependencies
Mexico, then, faces a problem that has less to do with its right to cooperate with China than with the coherence of its international strategy. It is contradictory to limit China’s economic presence in order to reduce friction with Washington while simultaneously deepening ties with Beijing in sectors that are far more sensitive to the United States.
China, moreover, is not Mexico’s only option for diversification. The modernized Mexico-European Union Global Agreement would allow more than 95 percent of Mexican exports to enter tariff-free into a market of 450 million people. Mexico could also make better use of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) or revitalize the Pacific Alliance, whose enlargement has remained stalled, among other reasons, by the diplomatic rupture with Ecuador following the 2024 raid on the Mexican Embassy in Quito. More ambitious commercial ties with Mercosur could complement these efforts.
None of these alternatives will replace the United States – the destination of more than 80 percent of Mexican exports. Nor could China, for that matter. But stronger ties with Europe, the Asia-Pacific, and Latin America could gradually reduce Mexico’s dependence without placing the country in the middle of the most contentious areas of China-U.S. competition.
Autonomy does not mean replacing one dependency with another, much less antagonizing Washington simply to demonstrate that Mexico can do so. Maintaining close relations with China is perfectly compatible with an independent foreign policy, but Mexico cannot ignore the costs of cooperation in sensitive areas. Trading with China is not the same as partnering with Beijing on digital infrastructure, semiconductors, or artificial intelligence.
