As with its ongoing fight against the former ambassador to the United Kingdom, who declared for the resistance and refused to leave the ambassador’s London residence since the coup, the Myanmar government has likely gauged that the time is ripe to intensify its campaign against Kyaw Moe Tun.
articles.summary: Naypyidaw is seeking the replacement of Kyaw Moe Tun, who pledged his loyalty to the opposition after the 2021 coup.

articles.title: AI, Robotics and the Coming Economic, Military, and Political Revolutions
articles.full_text:
In the context of ongoing transformations to the economy, society, and military, China’s current strategy is particularly alarming, and potentially transformational.
A humanoid service robot as a cashier in an automated convenience store selling drinks in Shanghai, China, Nov. 28, 2025.
As China’s President Xi Jinping prepares to travel to Washington, D.C. on September 24, his approach will reflect not only the specific items on his agenda, but also broader geopolitical transformations currently underway. These revolutions-in-progress create both enormous opportunities for China and hazards for it, and the international community, to navigate.
Reinforcing advances currently underway in “big data,” artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous systems, and robotics are rapidly transforming both economic and military dynamics, with radical implications for political systems and the global balance of power. Latin America and the rest of the developing world will be a battleground, a beneficiary, and a victim in that enormous and chaotic change.  
Although the future cannot be predicted with certainty, one reasonable outcome of the current confluence of trends is a world that is far more violent, less democratic, and more dominated by China. That future could emerge more rapidly than most traditional analysts expect. Here’s how such traumatic and revolutionary change could occur, and what it could mean for the United States, Latin America, and the world.
Within the next decade, developments arising out of the synergy between artificial intelligence and robotics will likely present non-human alternatives to a wide variety of both white-collar and blue-collar, skilled and unskilled labor, transforming a far broader range of work, far more rapidly than occurred in last century’s industrial revolution. The amortized cost of industrial robots is already less in many cases than employing a human to do the task.  
Mass-produced Chinese robots from companies like Unitree and UBTech can be ordered for as little as $5,000, with many industrial capable units costing only $20,000-$50,000. At that price, such a robot, capable of replacing three shifts of factory workers, costs only a few months of the human wages its use would save. As with personal computers in the 1990s, those costs will only come down, and the sophistication of hardware, firmware, and AI-powered “control” mechanisms will only improve, as robotic systems are deployed at scale in an increasingly broad range of tasks.
What makes the current revolution even more transformational is that increasingly capable AI tools, whether virtual or embodied, have the capability to replace humans not only in factory work, but also in domestic and service work, as well as white collar tasks. This is particularly the case in technical areas, such as computer programming, legal work, medical technicians, and administrative support staff, among others. It is highly likely, as Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, has said, that the nature of work will change from human beings doing things to directing and supervising AI and robotic systems in such tasks.  
Yet it is highly unlikely that the number of “supervisory” jobs created in the new AI-robotic economy, combined with new kinds of work supporting or complementing that economy, will fully offset those human jobs rendered economically non-competitive. The World Economic Forum estimates that current developments could displace 92 million jobs by 2030 alone. Moreover, the speed of the onset of the new tech economy, and the inherent difficulty of human beings adapting to new types of skills in new places, will significantly and rapidly expand what 19th century philosopher Thomas Robert Malthus once chillingly referred to as a “redundant population.”
As with the industrial revolution, the AI-robotics revolution will also likely expand socioeconomic inequality between those owning, implementing, and managing the structures of the new AI-robotics economy, and those whose jobs are replaced, or sectors whose wages are decreased, by competition with new AI and robotic alternatives. Those effects will be particularly acute among populations already increasingly discontent with democratic political systems’ dysfunction and inability to address contemporary challenges.
The responses of different political systems to such pressures will likely reflect a combination of two impulses: compensation and repression. Some governments will create or expand social “safety nets” to retrain, relocate, or at least mitigate the suffering of those displaced. Other governments – or in some cases, the same ones – will use instruments of state repression against those who react to the stresses caused by such economic displacement through descent into common criminality, or alternatively, violent protest and terrorism. Ironically, the tools for monitoring and controlling population’s movements, finances, and other aspects of their livelihood are also being greatly strengthened by advances in AI, access to “big data,” and other technologies. 
As AI puts significant pressures on democratic political systems and market economies, it will also play an ever-more-important role in the distribution, and ultimately, allocation, of resources for populations. Even today, AI is being used in operational management and logistics for both firms and governments. AI could actually mitigate some of the distortions and inefficiencies historically associated with government-led economic systems, most eloquently argued in 1945 by Friedrick Hayek. AI may thus help China and other authoritarian governments outcompete democratic free market systems by helping their performance, as well as their repressive capabilities, even as technology disruption dramatically expands stresses on democracies and market-based systems.
In tandem with such economic and political transformation, the aforementioned technology advances are also accelerating a revolution in military affairs. AI-enabled autonomous systems will increasingly replace manned ones in the air, on and under the ground, and in and under the water. They will be increasingly coordinated by AI-enabled battle and logistics management systems, whose ability to rapidly identify patterns and consider the outcome of numerous response scenarios will give them significant advantages over “human-in the loop” systems.  
At the same time, the new technologies will give middle powers, small states, and even resource-rich non-state criminal and terrorist groups the ability to defy and extort much larger actors, as Iran has done to the United States with its drone and missile systems.
In the context of such transformations, China’s current strategy is particularly alarming, and potentially transformational. On one hand, as seen previously in other technologies such as electric vehicles, Beijing has dedicated significant resources to dominating developments in AI and robotics. Repeating a tried-and-true blueprint, China has significantly invested in basic and applied research, protected and subsidized key enabling technology sectors, and leveraged China’s enormous captive internal market, in order to develop commercial products that could dominate in the global arena. 
In the present case, China is seeking to lead the world on AI by developing efficient, open-weight models such as Kimi K3, Deep Seek V4, and Qwen 3.8, even where its companies do not have access to the highest performance chips such as Nvidia Vera Rubin and Blackwell. While Chinese models are still modestly inferior to frontier Western models such as Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, ChatGPT 6 Astra, and Grok flagship, over the long term, the open-source nature of China’s models and their ability to function with lower performance chips positions them to dominate global markets such as those of Latin America, Africa, and developing Asia, even if they are excluded from the United States and Europe.   
Following a path similar to its approach to dominating other sectors of the global economy, China is now leveraging its control over its domestic market to introduce new leading edge capabilities with AI-enabled robots before market forces fully demand them. China is, for example, deliberately integrating AI-enabled robotics in factories and other domestic applications, giving it an edge over Western competitors such as Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robots, which may be marginally more sophisticated, but are still largely in the prototyping phase.
As occurred in electric vehicles, telecommunications, and solar panels and other strategic sectors before them, in AI-enabled robotics, China appears on track to use the ever-more capable, low-cost products it is developing in its internal market, and beginning to export, to beat out U.S. competitors in third markets such as Latin America.  
Even if the U.S. and European markets remain protected against the entry of Chinese AI models and AI-enabled robots and other systems, China is on track to be the dominant supplier of those AI models, robots, and systems in global markets within a decade. By extension, it could become the dominant producer of those systems at industrial scale. As occurred in telecommunications with companies such as Huawei, this situation would leave the United States to express concern over the real dangers that use of Chinese AI and robotics systems entailed, and to warn and threaten partners, without any good options to present commercially competitive alternatives.
Such a dominant Chinese position in AI and robotics would exponentially multiply Beijing’s already enormous leverage over the global economy and political dynamics. China already increasingly uses its power as a major commodities purchaser and infrastructure operator to coerce governments that act against its companies and strategic interests. Major recent examples include deliberate targeting of Panamanian flagged vessels for excessive inspections, following Panama’s Supreme Court decision against China-based firm Hutchinson. Beijing also threatened not to renew Argentina’s currency swap agreement after its president said he would not do business with “Chinese communists.” 
Along with Beijing’s greatly expanded economic and political leverage, to the extent robots, autonomous vehicles, and AI-enabled military management systems are key to success in future military operations, China’s dominance of those industries, combined with the industrial capability to produce millions of robots, would vastly accelerate its dominant military position and ability to sustain and reconstitute such a force. 
The strategic importance of a large industrial base has been dramatically illustrated in the role of Ukraine’s production of millions of drones amid its resistance against Russia’s invasion. It has also been illustrated in the U.S. need to replace the vast number of precision munitions expended in the Persian Gulf war, and in the ability of Chinese shipyards to produce 200 times more warships than the United States.
A future in which China vastly outpaces the United States as the arsenal of military robotics and autonomous systems would give Beijing a vast advantage not only in conducting and sustaining a conventional warfight with the U.S., but also in deploying such systems in defense of its array of its commercial and other interests abroad. In short, China’s domination of both the commercial and military dimension of the AI and robotics revolution could become the sustaining pillar as it transitions from cautious geopolitical competitor to “empire” with Chinese characteristics.
Growing Chinese power and influence will almost doubtlessly impact how Beijing behaves with respect to the United States and elsewhere.  Historically, where China has perceived itself weak, such as in areas geographically close to the U.S. in Latin America, Beijing has behaved with deference. Yet where it has perceived itself strong, such as in the South China Sea, it has behaved more aggressively. Illustrations include its militarization of reefs and shoals and enforcement of its “10-dashed-line” territorial claims there.  
The present global transition of power, with reinforcing technological, commercial, and military dimensions thus also implies a China emboldened to act more aggressively in Latin America, or even to act decisively to end Taiwan’s autonomy. Such actions and associated conflict would strongly affect the countries of the Western Hemisphere, including through the major disruptions in commerce and finance from a major war, not to mention likelihood that a supporting part of that war would be conducted in key terrain in the Western Hemisphere.
The forces unleashed by the interdependent and reinforcing revolutions in artificial intelligence and robotics more than transcend the specific discussions that will take place at the upcoming Trump-Xi summit. Nonetheless, that summit is coming at a symbolic and pivotal moment in which the technological and commercial advances and strategic decisions of both nations could precipitate rapid shifts in the relative power between them, and reshape the geopolitical environment for decades to come.
As China’s President Xi Jinping prepares to travel to Washington, D.C. on September 24, his approach will reflect not only the specific items on his agenda, but also broader geopolitical transformations currently underway. That future could emerge more rapidly than most traditional analysts expect. Here’s how such traumatic and revolutionary change could occur, and what it could mean for the United States, Latin America, and the world.

articles.title: SCO Summit Produces Surprising Winners
articles.full_text:
The organization’s smaller members can use a China-India-Russia-dominated forum without becoming subordinate to any single major power.
The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan August 31-September 1 marked a quarter century since the organization’s founding. Its anniversary motto, “Together for Sustainable Peace, Development and Prosperity,” hinted at ambitions considerably grander than the institution’s record. The SCO now encompasses ten member states, including China, India, Russia, Iran, Pakistan, and four Central Asian republics – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – representing nearly half of humanity and a substantial share of global economic activity.
Yet headlines emerging from Bishkek often highlighted the organization’s internal dynamics and differing national priorities. Unlike last year’s summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi did not hold a formal bilateral meeting, although their brief interaction during the summit quickly became a meme template among Indian netizens. Modi and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif traded predictable barbs. Most stunningly, Modi directly urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine “for humanity’s sake.” This comes shortly after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that China delivered an ultimatum to Russia not to use nuclear weapons in Ukraine, something China has not denied.
This focus on discord is not merely dramatic headline chasing; it reflects a genuine and consistently noted problem with the SCO. The organization brings together several geopolitical rivals. It is therefore difficult to imagine the institution ever evolving into a mirror of NATO. The SCO lacks the degree of institutionalization necessary to impose coherent policy on its members, while its principal powers lack sufficient leverage over one another to establish a common strategic direction.
But these features should not lead observers to dismiss the organization’s practical value for its members, especially the smaller ones. 
Institutionalization is a slow process, particularly among states with divergent political systems and strategic interests. The SCO already possesses permanent structures, including its Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) in Tashkent, while members continue to debate additional mechanisms for economic and security cooperation. 
The summit featured credible proposals for institutional development, including Xi proposing AI hubs, Uzbekistan proposing an industrial cooperation mechanism, Kyrgyzstan pushing its Tamchy Special Financial Investment Territory for joint SCO projects and advocating for Bishkek as the headquarters of a joint development bank, and Tajikistan pushing for a regional digital agro-ecological platform. 
Other developments emerged from the forum, especially multilateral initiatives in which the SCO serves not as an institutional organizer but as an exhibition hall for projects that individual governments want to pursue. 
This has created an unusual dynamic within the organization. While SCO’s largest powers are often stalemated by competing interests, institution-building initiatives that make the greatest practical progress frequently emerge because smaller member states want them to. 
SCO summits have increasingly become venues where host governments promote their own economic and diplomatic priorities. The pattern was particularly visible after the 2017 meeting in Astana. The massive Astana Expo opened the following day, underscoring how the summit could function as a platform for the host country’s broader international ambitions rather than simply as a meeting of an increasingly institutionalized organization.
Kyrgyzstan continued that tradition in Bishkek this year. As the outgoing chair and summit host, Bishkek had an obvious incentive to use the gathering to advance national priorities. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway received prominent attention. The project, a flagship Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) corridor running from Kashgar through Kyrgyzstan into Uzbekistan, has the potential to reshape the country’s position within Eurasian transportation networks. Kyrgyzstan also successfully promoted emerging trade routes connecting with India and Pakistan via China and the China Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and inked a deal to drastically increase trade with Pakistan.
Kyrgyzstan, like many smaller SCO members, appears interested in maximizing the benefits of participation without presenting itself as uncritically aligned with the organization’s largest powers. While Bishkek has been open about its close economic relationship with Beijing, it retains an interest in attracting capital from outside the SCO’s economic orbit. Western capital remains valuable precisely because it provides an alternative source of financing, expertise, and commercial relationships. The establishment of the Tamchy Special Financial and Investment Territory in 2025, a special economic zone which serves as an outpost of Western regulatory codes and law in the region, illustrates this broader effort to create a more attractive investment environment.
This behavior should not be interpreted as contradictory or even unique. For smaller SCO states, strategic ambiguity is an asset. Kyrgyzstan has no interest in choosing between China, Russia, India, and Western investors when it can instead extract advantages from all of them. The same logic explains why Central Asian governments routinely embrace Chinese infrastructure while simultaneously seeking European, American, Turkish, Gulf, Japanese, and South Korean investment. Their objective and chief concern is maintaining their own agency.
That agency may be one of the SCO’s most fascinating unintended characteristics. Multilateral institutions often develop institutional behaviors their founders did not explicitly design. The European Union, NATO, and ASEAN all have political cultures and operating assumptions that went beyond the intentions of their architects. The SCO appears to be developing something different: an environment in which its smaller members possess greater freedom of economic maneuver than the organization’s nominal power structure would suggest.
China, India, and Russia each have substantial reasons to use the SCO for their own strategic purposes. That divergence limits any one major power’s ability to turn the SCO into an instrument of strategic alignment.
China has the largest economy in the organization and increasingly supplies the infrastructure connecting its members. Russia retains military influence and longstanding political relationships. India possesses substantial economic and demographic weight while maintaining relationships with both Russia and the West. Yet, none can herd the others into an arrangement that systematically disadvantages the others or Western involvement.
The result is particularly visible in Central Asia. Governments there have little incentive to surrender their ability to balance among external powers. Chinese railways and investment can expand economic opportunity, while American or European capital can provide diversification. Turkish, Gulf, Indian, Japanese, and Korean partnerships provide additional options. For governments sitting between much larger powers, dependency on any single patron is inherently dangerous.
The SCO therefore produces a paradox. Its smaller members often determine whether any institutionalization actually moves forward. The major powers may act as veto-players or set strategic priorities, but implementation often depends on whether smaller governments see a direct benefit. It seems that the SCO’s largest members increasingly result to multilateral arrangements bypassing the SCO when convenient.
This is why Bishkek may ultimately prove more revealing than dramatic images of Modi, Xi, and Putin standing together. The central question is not whether the three largest powers can appear united, nor is it whether they can identify areas of common interest. The more important question is whether they can convert that shared interest into an institutional structure capable of constraining the strategic choices of the organization’s other members.
The organization’s most surprising winners are the states that were never expected to exercise much influence over it. Kyrgyzstan successfully used the summit and its 2025-2026 chairmanship to promote its economic priorities. Other small SCO states in Central Asia have long done the same, using the organization to attract capital, build connections, and preserve strategic options.
This is a very different outcome from the emergence of a unified Eurasian bloc or some grand anti-Western alliance some have predicted. For Washington, that distinction should matter. The SCO should not be dismissed as an ineffectual talking shop, but neither should it be treated as an embryonic anti-Western alliance with the activities of Beijing or Moscow ascribed to all of its members. Washington too would be better served by watching the multilateral announcements on the sidelines of the organization rather than taking grand declarations at face value.
So long as Beijing, New Delhi, and Moscow remain at loggerheads, they will be unable to impose a common strategic direction, and the organization’s smaller states will retain outsized influence and room to maneuver – particularly in the economic domain.
In Bishkek, that room was on display. The summit produced declarations, initiatives, infrastructure commitments, and political theater. More importantly, it showed that the organization’s smaller members can use a China-India-Russia-dominated forum without becoming subordinate to any single major power. The SCO may eventually become a more coherent institution. Until then, its greatest surprise is that the tail continues to wag the dog, and its smallest states, by converting membership into tangible development gains, are the biggest winners.

articles.title: What Role Does Denuclearization Have in North Korea-US Dialogue Today?
articles.full_text:
Breaking down the denuclearization debate from both sides: North Korea and the United States.
In this Feb. 27, 2019, file photo, then-U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at the Sofitel Legend Metropole hotel in Hanoi, Vietnam, for their second summit meeting.
With his surprise decision to scale back the recent Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercise on the Korean Peninsula, U.S. President Donald Trump clearly signaled his intent to rekindle dialogue with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. However, rather than receiving praise for the goodwill measure, the effort drew rebuke from the North Korean government, which reiterated its position that it has no interest in renewing engagement as long as the United States holds onto denuclearization as a policy objective.
This exchange has renewed debates over long-standing denuclearization policies, particularly as Trump continues his overtures toward the Kim regime in hopes of a possible meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in November. Some have argued it is time to abandon denuclearization as a policy goal and shift to arms control, while others contend that such a concession would undermine the global nonproliferation regime and place further stress on allied relationships.
Rather than a binary “should they, shouldn’t they” approach, the issue requires a more nuanced examination of the constraints and interests at play. For example, what does the Kim regime mean when it demands that foreign governments drop denuclearization as a precondition for talks? What does the Trump administration hope to achieve by renewing engagement? Further, would dropping denuclearization even be politically sustainable for this administration or other governments?
It’s useful to break down the denuclearization debate, examining the knowns and unknowns for the two sides.
Trump’s Overtures and North Korea’s Response
On August 16, Trump announced the shortening of the annual South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercise, reiterating his usual claim that the exercises are costly and adding that they “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea. He claimed that the Kim regime has been “unthreatening and respectful” during his presidency. 
North Korea’s response came on August 19 in the form of a statement attributed to Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s high-ranking sister. The statement declared that Pyongyang regarded the reduction of exercises as “unworthy of comment” and has “no interest in it at all” due to “the nature of the military drill with a provocative and offensive feature.” North Korea followed that up two weeks later with another statement attributed to an unnamed Foreign Ministry spokesperson, noting “it is pointless to expect any détente in the region” as the “U.S. remains committed to the complete denuclearization of the DPRK” (an abbreviation of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea). 
But this may be changing. In other contexts, the White House has demonstrated a willingness to abandon status quo policies and pursue rapprochement with authoritarian governments. As a result, the administration may consider shifting from denuclearization-first diplomacy to an approach that de-emphasizes denuclearization through arms control and risk reduction measures, or even eliminates it as a policy objective altogether. 
The Knowns and Unknowns of North Korean Demands
The Kim regime has clearly set a precondition for renewed engagement with the United States: drop denuclearization from the agenda. What is less clear is what North Korea actually expects with this precondition.  
Pyongyang’s rejections of denuclearization evolved following the brief period of diplomacy in 2018-19.  After the failure of Kim Jong Un and Trump to reach an agreement at the February 2019 Hanoi Summit, Pyongyang hardened its stance against denuclearization. In December 2019, North Korean Ambassador to the United Nations Kim Song stated that “denuclearization is already gone out of the negotiation table.” Based on numerous statements since, North Korea’s position has become more absolute: denuclearization is not up for negotiation and Pyongyang has no intention to relinquish its nuclear arms. 
Despite the hardline position, the Kim regime has not shut the door completely on potential engagement. North Korea has continued to highlight the “excellent” relationship between Kim Jong Un and Trump, referencing Kim’s “good memories and feelings” towards the U.S. president. Although positive inclinations in a personal relationship do not necessarily translate to rapprochement between governments, these are notable signals that may compel Washington to pursue status quo-changing pathways to engagement. 
A challenge for Washington is that the scope of the required policy change is not yet clear. What specific actions would Pyongyang expect from Washington to signal the end of denuclearization? Does this mean a policy pronouncement, rescission of United Nations Security Council resolutions, or something else? 
It is also unclear whether the Kim regime would be willing to offer concessions in return. There is no indication thus far of what may be negotiable with denuclearization off the agenda, whether it be arms control or other tradeoffs such as reducing North Korea’s military aid to Russia. This creates a risk: if the United States does give ground on denuclearization, Pyongyang could simply walk away from dialogue since it has already met one of its key policy objectives.
On the U.S. side, there is a growing recognition that North Korea’s nuclear capability is now an established reality. Three decades of efforts to persuade Pyongyang to relinquish its nuclear weapons have not curbed the Kim regime’s ability to develop a nuclear weapons program of considerable scale and capability. Trump recently said North Korea has 57 warheads, while the South Korean Ministry of National Defense estimated it to be somewhere between 80 and 120.
From the outset, the United States’ goal has been to achieve a nuclear-free peninsula through diplomatic means. This has contributed to a substantial body of policies, sanctions, and international resolutions aimed at constraining and ultimately eliminating the North Korea nuclear program. Thus, there are significant legal and political considerations that affect the extent to which Washington can pursue alternate approaches. 
One consideration is the global nonproliferation regime. A shift in U.S. policy would have ripple effects across the framework designed to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, including the Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference and the International Atomic Energy Agency. Experts have pointed out that abandoning denuclearization would signal a de facto acceptance of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state, and that risks not only undermining the Non-Proliferation Treaty but setting a precedent for other rogue states to pursue nuclear armament.
Also, the United States and the U.N. Security Council have imposed numerous rounds of sanctions on North Korea in response to its nuclear development and testing activities, in part to mitigate the increase in nuclear weapons while also deterring others from pursuing similar programs. A formal policy shift that accepted North Korea as a nuclear-armed state would raise questions about the status of existing sanctions and internationally agreed-upon resolutions. At the U.N. level, alterations to the North Korea sanctions program would require Security Council action, potentially requiring the modification or termination of existing resolutions that could easily be blocked by a veto from France, the United Kingdom, or any of the other five permanent members of the Security Council. 
A second consideration is the response from U.S. allies. Most American allies and partners have established policies supporting a nuclear-free North Korea, so any unilateral U.S. decision will have cascading effects, forcing other governments either to adapt to a policy shift or oppose the U.S. approach. This will be particularly important for South Korea and Japan. 
Although Seoul has already placed denuclearization as the last step of its “END” strategy (“Exchange, Normalization, Denuclearization”) it has not dropped it as a goal altogether. Meanwhile, Japan’s commitment to North Korea’s complete denuclearization remains a pillar of its security designs. A change would push Tokyo to assess how much policy space exists within its current framework to move closer to Washington’s or Seoul’s approach. It may be possible for the three to retain a formal commitment to denuclearization while also pursuing nuclear risk reduction and arms controls, but there will invariably be an impact to trilateral cooperation that requires close coordination. 
Further, any pursuit of diplomatic engagement with North Korea without addressing the Kim regime’s ongoing support for Russia’s war effort against Ukraine will invariably face opposition from the United States’ European allies. These partners may withhold support outright unless the White House is willing to leverage issues related to the Russia-Ukraine War in pursuit of engagement with Pyongyang.
The third factor is domestic politics. While the Trump administration was able to move forward on controversial decisions in the first half of his term, the forthcoming midterm election could bring to power a Democratic-controlled Congress, which would attempt more restraint. Additionally, groups across the political spectrum are opposed to altering denuclearization policy, calling into question the sustainability of such a change. Notably, Trump cannot run for re-election; the coming change in presidential administration after 2028 could result in an outright policy reversal.
What This Tells Us About the Denuclearization Debate
These knowns and unknowns reveal a few key considerations for the denuclearization debate.
To start, it would be useful to canvas North Korea about what it actually means by dropping denuclearization as a policy objective. In other words, if the White House is seeking meaningful engagement, a starting point can be inquiring about the Kim regime’s expectations for moving forward past denuclearization. This can be communicated through direct lines of communication or signaled through talking points in the media. 
It is also essential to identify the two sides’ goals if preconditions are met and talks happen. Right now, there is no clear indication of what the White House would be seeking to achieve through another summit between Trump and Kim Jong Un. Conversely, after more than 30 years of focusing on denuclearization, it is unclear what the Kim regime would be prepared to discuss in direct dialogue with the United States. Focused examinations and debates on these issues would be helpful in charting a course forward for any potential engagement.
Finally, it is necessary to determine how to translate goals into sustainable policy adjustments. The reality is that the U.S. and North Korea governments are different in nature, and while the Kim regime may be willing and able to institutionalize a permanent change to the status quo, conditions for a democratically-elected government are different. Unilaterally dropping denuclearization as a U.S. policy objective for a photo op will almost inevitably result in significant political pushback and challenges, both domestically and abroad. 
Ultimately, the denuclearization debate must be resolved if dialogue with North Korea remains an objective. However, if the goal is to ensure that the dialogue actually produces meaningful outcomes, the debate will require more nuance and structure than currently exist. What would this policy shift mean in practice? Can the White House build an engagement strategy that is realistic enough to produce useful dialogue with North Korea, ambitious enough to reduce nuclear risks, and durable enough to overcome the inevitable obstacles along the way?
articles.summary: Breaking down the denuclearization debate from both sides: North Korea and the United States.

articles.title: Can India Exploit China’s ‘Malacca Dilemma’?
articles.full_text:
New Delhi need not match Beijing militarily to impose disproportionate strategic costs.
A true-color image of the Strait of Malacca acquired on August 22, 2025, by the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) on NASA’s Aqua satellite.
India faces one of the most challenging security environments in the world, confronting not one but two adversarial neighbors: Pakistan and China. While New Delhi retains the conventional military upper hand over Islamabad, in Beijing it confronts a militarily and economically superior power that has repeatedly used force to alter the status quo along their disputed border.
Since the 1962 border war, India and China have faced a series of military confrontations, including the 2017 Doklam standoff and the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020. More recently, Beijing reportedly provided Islamabad with critical intelligence support during the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, raising the likelihood that any future Indo-Pak crisis will unfold against the backdrop of Chinese support for Islamabad.
Given this geopolitical reality, India must prepare to deter and, if needed, confront future Chinese aggression. Although formidable, India’s military remains conventionally weaker than China’s. At $92 billion, New Delhi’s defense spending is just over a quarter of Beijing’s. Despite India’s efforts to procure advanced Western fighter jets and develop its own indigenous capabilities, China still enjoys a 3:1 advantage in airpower, and its naval modernization far outpaces India’s own efforts.
Fortunately for India, it does not need to match China’s military capabilities one-to-one to establish credible deterrence. The ongoing conflict in the Gulf presents yet another lesson in how it can use asymmetric warfare to its advantage. Over the past six months, Iran has demonstrated its ability to threaten commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting global energy markets and imposing disproportionate costs on conventionally superior military powers.
China, too, has a major maritime vulnerability. Nearly 80 percent of its total energy imports, worth $312 billion, pass through the Strait of Malacca – the shortest sea route between the Middle East and East Asia – creating a critical maritime chokepoint. Recognizing this, China has invested heavily in mitigating the so-called “Malacca Dilemma,” but despite these efforts Beijing remains deeply exposed. Alternative waterways like Sunda and Lombok increase travel time, fuel costs, and logistical complexity, while land-based routes linked to the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are expensive and vulnerable to political instability. It is still critical for China that this vital sea lane remains open.
If it invests in the right maritime denial capabilities, New Delhi could exploit Beijing’s dependence on the Strait of Malacca to offset its conventional disadvantage, whether in a major conflict involving Chinese military aggression against India, or in a situation with more direct military involvement from Beijing in an Indo-Pak crisis. If it finds itself pulled into a broader Indo-Pacific contingency, New Delhi could even work in coordination with Western naval forces. 
Disrupting traffic through the Malacca Strait would carry considerable military and political risks. However, India need not close the strait to strengthen deterrence. The ability to credibly threaten such disruption could force Beijing to account for severe economic costs, underscoring the need for India to invest in maritime-denial capabilities now. To address regional concerns, India would need to frame these capabilities as part of a broader effort to strengthen deterrence in the Indo-Pacific, ideally in coordination with regional partners rather than over their heads.
Such a strategy would hinge on a layered maritime-denial architecture. India’s control of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands means it does not need to rely on expensive aircraft carriers to threaten shipping through the Malacca Strait. Instead, it could use low-cost unmanned systems of the kind Iran has employed to deter Chinese vessels and alter the cost-benefit calculus for China. 
Similarly, India could utilize inexpensive naval mines to complicate maritime access; the psychological impact of a mined waterway alone can be sufficient to deter vessels carrying expensive cargoes. 
The Indian Navy’s submarines operating from the Bay of Bengal would be another valuable asset in such a scenario, not simply because they would put vessels at risk, but also because their presence would force Beijing to devote scarce resources to complex anti-submarine warfare operations.
New Delhi’s growing anti-ship cruise missile arsenal would add to the efficacy of such a layered area-denial architecture. India’s BrahMos and new long-range hypersonic anti-ship missile could threaten Chinese ships from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands without putting expensive naval destroyers in harm’s way.  
To make the strategy credible, however, India would need more than just these individual assets. It would need persistent intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance across the eastern Indian Ocean; resilient command-and-control networks; and regular military exercises that demonstrate an ability to integrate drones, submarines, mines, and missiles into a coherent maritime denial strategy. 
While New Delhi has invested in expanding its arsenal of these individual assets, it still lacks a coherent maritime denial strategy for the Strait of Malacca. Such an objective would be better served, for one, by fortifying the Andaman and Nicobar Command with credible military capabilities – an undertaking that should not be conflated with the Great Nicobar Island Project. The project has evident dual-use dimensions, but it remains primarily a commercial infrastructure initiative and should not be treated as a substitute for hard military power.
China has spent decades trying to resolve the Malacca Dilemma because Beijing understands its vulnerability. India should recognize that same reality. It need not match China ship for ship or aircraft for aircraft. By investing in credible maritime denial capabilities around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, New Delhi can ensure that any Chinese aggression carries costs Beijing cannot ignore.

articles.title: The Mecca Pact: A New Treaty Organization, Just Like the Old One
articles.full_text:
MJDA is much like the Cold War’s CENTO and is likely to be just as impactful.
Much has been made of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement (MJDA) – a collective security agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye in early August – in news and analysis recently. Some have likened this to the Russia-dominated Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO). Others have called this a signal of the end of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and the birth of a new regional order. Though, perhaps reports of NATO’s death are greatly exaggerated. 
And with the benefit of a longer historical lens, we can see how prognostications that MJDA will remake the region’s  security are fairly off the mark. More than anything, MJDA resembles the failed and somewhat forgotten Central Treaty Organization (CENTO) of the Cold War. And, we can expect that, like CENTO, the member states themselves, and those around them, will continue their defense and security planning much as they have before. MJDA is unlikely to solve the problems it purports to confront and will accomplish little more than the Cold War’s CENTO. For a closer modern analogue, perhaps look to the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) structure, a forum for warm promises and suppressed disgruntlement.
But for a moment, let’s turn back the clock. CENTO was launched as the Baghdad Pact in 1955, a defensive agreement between Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkiye (then spelled Turkey), and the United Kingdom, with the United States initially serving as an observer. This was a reaction to the failing World War II global alliance system and the emergence of new security challenges – specifically, the split between capitalism and communism. 
Regionally, secular powers in and around the Middle East feared that a reemergent Soviet Union would follow the path of tsarist Russia. They anticipated that a desire for warm-water ports and hydrocarbons (mainly oil at the time) would drive Moscow’s perceived designs on the Mediterranean Sea, the Persian Gulf, and even the Indian Ocean. So, by encouraging this alliance, Washington could extend First World containment well beyond the borders of NATO. This merged policy to theory that was expressed in the “Long Telegram,” providing “strong resistance” at a possible point where Soviets might probe.
Yet, almost as soon as the ink was dry on the treaty agreement, membership fractured. A military coup overthrew the Iraqi monarch and the country withdrew from the pact in 1958. A Ba’athist revolution shortly thereafter would sever any possible reconciliation with the U.S.-aligned group. And so the group (minus Baghdad) renamed itself CENTO. The alliance didn’t rate very highly years later. In 1963 a cement factory dedication took priority for the Pakistani president, during a summit held in Karachi.
CENTO did have other goals beyond defense. It was supposed to advance economic cooperation and trade, communications, and transportation links between the member states. This included the establishment of a joint nuclear research center in Tehran, supported by London. New communication links were designed with Washington funding construction to better connect Ankara, Tehran, and Karachi; Iran’s Chabahar was envisioned as providing a vital pivot for commerce and movement across the entire region. 
Yet, the central aim of CENTO was mutual defense against Soviet aggression. What did the pact provide for? In short, very little. The defense articles urged mutual cooperation, non-interference in internal affairs, and respect for pre-existing obligations, while leaving open the possibility of accession by other Arab League members. Spoiler: none joined. Only in bilateral deals did the treaty have teeth. Ultimately, the United States took on responsibility to resist outside aggression and provide military or economic assistance necessary to preserve member states’ independence.  
That didn’t really pan out as members looked to their own defense policies. Ultimately, the Soviets didn’t need to force their way through Iran. Moscow established links with Ba’athist governments in CENTO’s “rear,” for example, and built ties in Ethiopia and (then North) Yemen that exploited anti-colonial sentiment. Meanwhile, the United States sanctioned CENTO ally Turkiye in 1974 over the invasion of Cyprus. And in Pakistan’s wars with India, Turkiye and Iran were absent. Indeed, many of the security problems of the 1960s and ’70s that enmeshed CENTO states are still salient today.
All this elides the fact that Soviet leaders Nikita Khrushchev and Leonid Brezhnev had no intention of driving to the sea. The deployment of Soviet forces, regardless of ebbs and flows to U.S.-USSR bilateral relations, was focused on the NATO threat to the west and southwest. Recall, Soviet forces withdrew from Iran shortly after the war ended, and lost their oil concessions as well. The December 1979 invasion of Afghanistan was never predicated on a further push to the Indian Ocean. In sum, the actual security threats facing member states and the political aims of CENTO were misaligned. 
So, how about the MJDA today? The current global context does share some superficial similarities to global politics in the 1950s. As then, today the global order is rapidly transforming. A comfortable modus vivendi between the U.S., Europe, Russia, and China has not yet emerged. And proxy wars at these great powers’ frontiers are challenging the old order that had lasted through most of the Cold War and several decades after.
Yet, as with CENTO, the new MJDA is a treaty without teeth, between states with diverse security problems and little impetus to work together on those challenges. First off, Pakistan, as during CENTO and afterward, remains mired in low-grade conflict with India. India remains the primary threat to Pakistan and the reason that the latter has long sought strategic “depth” in Afghanistan. 
Second, Turkiye, despite trending to strongman governance and fickle defense policies that saw it purchase, then resell, S-400s from Russia, remains the largest ground force in NATO (on the continent). Indeed, Riyadh has little to offer Ankara in terms of conventional capabilities. And fighting around the Straits of Bab el-Mandeb or Hormuz has little impact on Turkiye’s energy revenues. The Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan Pipeline’s exports are healthy amid two ongoing wars in the Persian Gulf and eastern Europe.
Third, Saudi Arabia’s regional adventurism is not something that Pakistan or Turkiye are likely to back. Riyadh has the mistaken impression that expensive kit equals a capable military. But repeated aerial bombing of Houthi rebels has done little to turn the tide of that conflict. Pan-Arabism was watery mortar for CENTO and pan-Islamism is likely to prove just as undependable for MJDA.
Another key point: Pakistan and Turkiye already enjoy their own nuclear umbrellas. Pakistan’s survival is guaranteed by its nuclear force of some couple hundred nuclear warheads. Turkiye’s survival is guaranteed by NATO’s nuclear umbrella. Saudi Arabia is the odd partner out here – at least until it develops its own domestic program, something the current U.S. administration has promised to help with. 
Finally, what does the treaty itself commit the partners to? The MJDA, at this point, is a series of statements. Those statements claim that the treaty will consider an armed attack against one an attack against all signatories, and further defense cooperation between the signatories will be encouraged. The latter is so much diplomatese and nothing in previous bilateral agreements impeded such cooperation. 
The former commitment lacks credibility. Importantly, who is the enemy here? Iran? India? Israel? Al-Qaida? Islamic State affiliates? None of the participating states will commit their nuclear forces to a poorly defined enemy that the members don’t even share. As for conventional forces, certainly the member states can share what they are learning about air defenses and drone warfare. But will Ankara or Islamabad commit to defending Riyadh’s airspace? 
This commitment is likely to be tested sooner rather than later with the ongoing Iran-U.S. War. And the most likely outcome is stern statements, arms sales, and perhaps joint training events. 
CENTO disappeared because the supposed threat it was designed to confront – Soviet incursion toward southern ports – had to be contained, even though it was illusory and only faintly hinted at by George Kennan. MJDA, if indeed aimed against Iranian “hegemony,” is trying to similarly commit states to a defense that they don’t share and misplaced security perceptions. 
Much like CENTO, MJDA members just don’t share the same security threats nor do they have the will to commit to mutual defense. Today, there’s not even a foreign policy push from a great or super power behind this alliance. Twenty years from now we will probably talk about MJDA just as much Cold Warriors thought about CENTO a generation after it was formed: not much.

articles.title: Learning Chinese Sign Language
articles.full_text:
There are multiple different sign languages – some of which are not easily intelligible to deaf people.
Learning Chinese Sign Language is a bewildering experience. To begin with, Chinese Sign Language (CSL) is in itself best understood as an umbrella term rather than a well-defined language. 
You have Signed Chinese, shoushi hanyu, which is one-to-one transcriptions of the written standard Chinese into signs, replete with interpuncation such as signed question marks. Then there is Natural Sign Language, ziran shouyu, the language that is actually spoken between native deaf signers in China. It has syntax and grammar markedly different from Chinese, makes extensive use of abbreviations and, like all natural sign languages, incorporates facial expressions. 
Besides these, there are yet other types of CSL described in the academic literature, such as Literary Sign Language (wenfa shouyu) and Society Sign Language (shehui shouyu). All the more confusing is how these terms often seem to overlap or even are used interchangeably.
Since 2018, the government has been actively promoting a type of sign language titled Guojia Tongyong Shouyu, sometimes translated into English as Chinese General Sign Language (CGSL). According to the Chinese Ministry of Education, CGSL can be seen as the sign language equivalent to Standard Mandarin. Having moved away from a standard based on spoken or written Chinese, CGSL incorporates elements from the natural sign languages and thus appears to be less alien to native deaf speakers. While this standardized variety has been described by some Chinese academics as a “natural sign language,” it is, however, uncertain if it is viewed as such by deaf Chinese themselves. 
For the prospective learner, there is a surprisingly user-friendly app based on the official CGSL lexicon. There are daily quizzes, signed demonstrations of the words, targeted tests, themed glossaries, and other useful tools for learning. Unfortunately, all of this does not compensate for the staggering lack of lexemes in the dictionary. Basic and commonly used words such as “curious” or “already” are missing. 
Sometimes the all too familiar top-down perspective of Chinese officialdom shines through with its clear political priorities: while there is an entry for “Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League,” the arguably far more useful word “weekend” is not listed. Even more striking is how words pertaining to sexuality or “taboo” body parts are missing altogether. For example, how would a sign language interpreter fare at a client’s gynecologist visit when the CGSL has no official terms for a woman’s genitalia? 
A couple of years ago, I was myself trying to learn Chinese Sign Language. I began by signing up to an online class, taught for free three nights a week. The teacher, however, was of the old-school, pre-CGSL era. Each lesson he stiffly taught us how to sign Chinese words and characters, without any facial cues and without teaching any grammar. Knowing enough about sign language to recognize that this was not the way deaf Chinese actually speak to each other, I quickly abandoned this approach and figured that the best way would be to befriend native speakers and simply learn from them. 
What I had not foreseen was how the natively spoken natural sign languages not only vary from region to region, but seemingly even from speaker to speaker. Without classroom instruction and with different speakers signing in different ways, it soon became hard to know which was the “correct” way to sign. Apparently, I was not the only one with this problem: one of my deaf acquaintances said he would often not understand what other native deaf speakers were saying. 
In fact, not only do deaf Chinese sometimes have a hard time understanding each other, but most of them struggle to understand the sign language used in official Chinese media. In one study exploring this issue, up to 84 percent of the deaf participants reported having trouble understanding the signed Chinese in television programs. 
Phenomena such as these – official use of sign language that is unintelligible for actual deaf persons – might, in some part, be ascribed to what in Chinese is called xingshi zhuyi, or pointless formalism. The 2008 Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Protection of Disabled Persons stated that there should be sign language available for television shows, and state-owned broadcasting companies might simply want to check that box – without bothering to produce content that is relevant for or even comprehensible to a deaf audience. 
With this said, there is an apparent growing interest among Chinese academics, and clear signs of growing awareness of sign language issues in Chinese society in general. My experiences with learning Chinese Sign Language might already be outdated. In 2023, a long article with the title “The Sign Language Used by Interpreters Is 90 Percent Incomprehensible to Deaf People” ran in the well-renowned Shanghai-based publication The Paper. According to state media, a national standard for proficiency and testing in CGSL has been implemented since March last year. Things are looking up. 
Some of the most exciting developments, however, are taking place on social media. On platforms such as WeChat and Xiaohongshu (RedNote), there are countless content creators discussing the differences between different types of sign language, teaching sign language to others, or poking fun at the stiff, unnatural mimicry of hearing learners. 
Surprisingly enough, some deaf users are also openly discussing governmental policies, seizing a rare opportunity for a marginalized group to talk about the political reforms directly affecting them. That these topics apparently have a low level of political sensitivity might, however, not be something to view entirely as a positive. Perhaps it simply speaks to the level of neglect of the deaf community. 
Nevertheless, the days of “Signed Chinese” seem to be numbered, and younger generations of media-savvy deaf Chinese might quickly become a force to be reckoned with. One could venture to say that the future is looking bright for new learners of Chinese Sign Language.

In one study exploring this issue, up to 84 percent of the deaf participants reported having trouble understanding the signed Chinese in television programs. 
Phenomena such as these – official use of sign language that is unintelligible for actual deaf persons – might, in some part, be ascribed to what in Chinese is called xingshi zhuyi, or pointless formalism. The 2008 Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Protection of Disabled Persons stated that there should be sign language available for television shows, and state-owned broadcasting companies might simply want to check that box – without bothering to produce content that is relevant for or even comprehensible to a deaf audience. 
With this said, there is an apparent growing interest among Chinese academics, and clear signs of growing awareness of sign language issues in Chinese society in general. My experiences with learning Chinese Sign Language might already be outdated. In 2023, a long article with the title “The Sign Language Used by Interpreters Is 90 Percent Incomprehensible to Deaf People” ran in the well-renowned Shanghai-based publication The Paper. According to state media, a national standard for proficiency and testing in CGSL has been implemented since March last year. Things are looking up. 
Some of the most exciting developments, however, are taking place on social media. On platforms such as WeChat and Xiaohongshu (RedNote), there are countless content creators discussing the differences between different types of sign language, teaching sign language to others, or poking fun at the stiff, unnatural mimicry of hearing learners. 
Surprisingly enough, some deaf users are also openly discussing governmental policies, seizing a rare opportunity for a marginalized group to talk about the political reforms directly affecting them. That these topics apparently have a low level of political sensitivity might, however, not be something to view entirely as a positive. Perhaps it simply speaks to the level of neglect of the deaf community. 
Nevertheless, the days of “Signed Chinese” seem to be numbered, and younger generations of media-savvy deaf Chinese might quickly become a force to be reckoned with. One could venture to say that the future is looking bright for new learners of Chinese Sign Language. 
Learning Chinese Sign Language is a bewildering experience. To begin with, Chinese Sign Language (CSL) is in itself best understood as an umbrella term rather than a well-defined language.
articles.summary: There are multiple different sign languages – some of which are not easily intelligible to deaf people.

articles.title: Bangladesh and the Perils of Pax Silica
articles.full_text:
It could end up exchanging strategic flexibility for an upgraded version of the subcontracting economy it is trying to escape.
U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor with Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at a meeting in Dhaka, Bangladesh, August 1, 2026.
On August 1, U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor presented a consequential proposition to Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to join Pax Silica. “The country has significant potential to become a partner in the global economic security alliance focused on artificial intelligence, semiconductors and critical mineral supply chains,” he said.
On the same day, Dhaka announced that it would join the Shanghai-based World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), initially as an observer. Bangladesh therefore found itself courted by two emerging technology orders in a single news cycle. The invitation deserves neither reflexive rejection nor diplomatic applause. It demands a national strategy. What, then, should Bangladesh do?
Pax Silica was launched in Washington in December 2025 with seven declaration signatories to “build a secure, prosperous, and innovation-driven silicon supply chain — from critical minerals and energy inputs to advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, AI infrastructure and logistics.” By mid-August 2026, 25 countries, including the U.S., U.K., Japan, Singapore and India, had signed on.
Pax Silica is not simply about chips. Its ambition covers the full artificial intelligence stack: minerals, refining, electricity, data infrastructure, semiconductor design and production, logistics, advanced manufacturing, models, and digital platforms. The State Department describes the goal as reducing coercive dependencies and creating trusted supply chains.
The geopolitical interest is equally clear. It seeks to reorganize strategic technology networks to reduce dependence on China. The initiative has already moved beyond diplomatic language. Washington announced a $250 million Pax Silica Fund for mineral processing, infrastructure, and manufacturing. It has supported plans for a 4,000-acre economic security zone in the Philippines, launched a $1.5 billion artificial intelligence investment platform with Southeast Asia, and partnered with Stanford University on an advanced manufacturing curriculum for participating economies. For allied countries, the promise is access to capital, skills, technology networks, trusted markets, and greater protection from supply disruptions.
China’s response has taken both institutional and commercial form. Beijing continues to criticize exclusive blocs and defends open supply chains, while retaining powerful leverage through its dominance of critical mineral processing and selective export controls. It has also backed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which presents itself as a development-focused and more inclusive alternative.
Pax Silica may not name China, but the rivalry is no longer implicit. Washington is increasingly asking partners to align their technology ecosystems with one side or the other.
Bangladesh has reasons to explore the offer. Its economy was worth about $456 billion in 2025, and its large domestic market gives it commercial weight. Bangladesh has about 700 chip designers, more than 20,000 annual graduates in computer science and electrical engineering, and a small semiconductor design services industry earning roughly $8 million a year. The government created a national semiconductor task force in 2025, with design, verification, testing, and packaging identified as realistic entry points.
Pax Silica appears to offer Bangladesh a chance to move beyond its garment-dominated export economy by linking local firms and universities with partners in the U.S., Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore, and Europe. Benefits include training, joint research, cybersecurity standards, and cleaner energy finance. Rather than aiming for advanced fabrication, Bangladesh could focus on chip design, testing, packaging, and AI applications. Its Bay of Bengal location, ports, and workforce could provide geostrategic leverage, reducing vulnerability and increasing bargaining power.
However, strategic location is not readiness. Bangladesh’s current capabilities remain far below the level required to bargain as an equal partner. Semiconductor exports of $8 million are tiny beside the announced $1 billion target for 2030. Reliable, affordable electricity remains a national challenge. During the 2026 energy crisis, the government even closed universities early to conserve power. Advanced electronics and data infrastructure require uninterrupted electricity, clean water, specialized chemicals, strong intellectual property rules, cybersecurity, rapid customs clearance, and credible environmental regulation.
The Philippines demonstrates why readiness must come before ambition. Manila joined Pax Silica in April and announced a 4,000-acre hub in New Clark City. The project soon faced demands for Senate scrutiny and public consultation, along with criticism from scientists, farmers, environmental groups, and Indigenous communities. Estimates circulated in the Philippine policy debate suggested that the hub could eventually require 3 gigawatts of electricity and about 130 million liters of water a day.
Concerns also arose over land rights, long leases, waste, transparency, and the distribution of benefits. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. publicly defended the project. The lesson is not that the Philippine project will fail. It is that a technology coalition cannot substitute for domestic state capacity. Announcing a hub before establishing its energy, water, legal, environmental, and social foundations turns an economic opportunity into a political backlash. Bangladesh should absorb that warning, given its own fragile utilities and limited research capacity.
There is a second danger. Bangladesh could enter Pax Silica not as a technology partner but as a low-cost labor and land platform. Multinational firms might place assembly, testing, or support services in the country while keeping design authority, patents, procurement, and profits abroad. World Bank research on global value chains shows that technology spillovers depend on the absorptive capacity of local firms, supplier linkages, skills, and deliberate policy. Foreign investment alone does not guarantee industrial upgrading.
Alliance theory warns that Bangladesh risks trading autonomy for limited benefits in Pax Silica. Morrow’s asymmetric alliance model shows weaker states often concede policy freedom, while Keohane’s reciprocity norm stresses mutual gains. Bangladesh currently offers geography and labor but little scarce technology, weakening its bargaining power. True readiness, including local research, training, and supplier development, is essential for negotiating durable, reciprocal partnerships.
Bangladesh has long sought strategic autonomy. Bangladesh also joined China’s new artificial intelligence organization as an observer on the very day Gor raised Pax Silica. Full participation in both systems may be possible while commitments remain loose, but that space could narrow as standards and security rules harden.
The same dangers apply if Bangladesh joins the Chinese camp. WAICO could pressure Dhaka to adopt Chinese vendors, standards, and data rules, leaving Bangladesh with little bargaining power. Since Chinese firms already dominate its power, transport, and telecom sectors, deeper alignment risks greater dependency. It could also reduce Western access to capital and markets. The real issue is Bangladesh’s weak technological base, which makes it vulnerable whichever side it chooses.

articles.title: Namal Rajapaksa’s Arrest and Sri Lanka’s Politics of Mutual Protection
articles.full_text:
The old establishment elites have opposed Namal’s arrest. They want to preserve a system where one of their own is not jailed for corruption.
Sri Lanka Podujana Party parliamentarian Namal Rajapaksa waves to his supporters in the Tissamaharama electorate of Hambantota District, Sri Lanka, Aug. 29, 2026.
Sri Lankan investigators arrested Namal Rajapaksa on September 4 over allegations that he received 100 million Sri Lankan rupees (about $800,000 per 2014-15 exchange rates) in bribes linked to an aircraft procurement deal involving SriLankan Airlines in 2012-13.
The arrest shows that investigators have moved beyond airline officials and business intermediaries to a member of Sri Lanka’s most powerful political family.
The reaction to the arrest was interesting. The United National Party (UNP), which led the 2015-19 Yahapalanaya (good governance) government under which several investigations against Rajapaksa began, joined the Rajapaksa family-led Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna (SLPP) in condemning his arrest. Their response also demonstrates why a political party from outside the UNP-SLPP establishment needed to be in power to pursue investigations against powerful politicians.
Most of the political opposition and their allies in the media and religious establishments have come out in support of the Rajapaksas, and enormous resources are being spent to discredit the arrest of Namal. Thus, the question is not merely whether Namal will be convicted, but whether the National People’s Power (NPP) anti-corruption campaign can survive contact with the same political pressures that neutered every previous attempt to hold Sri Lanka’s elites to account.
In 2020, Airbus agreed to pay nearly $4 billion to settle international bribery investigations. As part of the investigations, foreign officials traced suspicious payments linked to SriLankan Airlines’ aircraft purchases, and a British court made details of the transactions public. In response, the Gotabaya Rajapaksa government arrested former SriLankan Airlines CEO Kapila Chandrasena and his wife. But the investigation went no further; the two were released on bail, and no action was taken to determine whether Chandrasena and others worked with politicians.
Even in 2020, authorities knew that part of the money had been sent to a company connected to businessman Nimal Perera, who was closely associated with the Rajapaksas. Yet neither the Gotabaya Rajapaksa administration (2019-2022) nor the Ranil Wickremesinghe administration (2022-2024) investigated what Perera did with the money. That investigation was only initiated after the NPP came into power.
The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) told the court that 1.454 million euros (or $1.69 million as per the September 2026 exchange rate) in bribe money was deposited into a Standard Chartered Bank account in Singapore maintained by Biz Solutions Inc., a company registered in Brunei and controlled by Chandrasena’s wife. Of that amount, $800,000 was allegedly transferred to an Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited (OCBC) account in Singapore maintained by Sabre Vision Holdings Ltd., a company belonging to Perera. Investigators allege that Perera converted the money into Sri Lankan rupees and handed it to Namal Rajapaksa in several installments during 2014 and 2015.
After investigations began under the NPP, investigators traveled to Australia, where Perera now lives, and obtained a sworn affidavit from him. He reportedly refused to return to Sri Lanka because of alleged threats to his life but told investigators that he had handed the rupee equivalent of the $800,000 to Namal Rajapaksa.
Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara also told the court that CIABOC and the Criminal Investigation Department had conducted a joint investigation with assistance from Australia, Singapore, France, and the United States. Airbus officials had also visited the commission several times. An Airbus delegation was in Colombo as recently as August to assist investigators.
These collaborations give the case a stronger foundation. The foreign banking records and international cooperation cannot easily be dismissed as inventions of the NPP. But the most important part of the allegation, i.e., that the money ultimately reached Namal, depends heavily on Perera’s testimony.
President’s Counsel Sampath Mendis, appearing for Namal, argued that neither Airbus officials nor French investigators had accused his client of receiving money. He also questioned Perera’s credibility.
The SLPP had planned a rally under Rajapaksa’s leadership in Anuradhapura on September 12, and the party alleged that the arrest was designed to disrupt its mobilization and weaken its national organizer.
The UNP, which once claimed to be arch-enemies of the Rajapaksas, came to Namal’s aid. It condemned the arrest as an attempt to sabotage the SLPP rally and insisted that Namal had the same democratic right as President Anura Dissanayake to travel around the country and hold public meetings. Wickremesinghe said that with Namal’s arrest, the government was weakening the opposition and threatening Sri Lanka’s democratic system.
The UNP’s response is ironic as investigations into Namal and other members of his family began during the UNP-led Yahapalanaya government. Ever since the Rajapaksas came into power in 2005, the UNP (the main opposition party at the time) insisted that they were a rogue and corrupt political dynasty that is undermining democracy, the rule of law, and the independence of institutions.
When the UNP-led Yahapalanaya administration came to power in 2015, a number of probes were launched against the Rajapaksas. Financial crime investigators arrested Namal twice in 2016 in connection with separate money-laundering allegations. But as with many cases filed during the Yahapalanaya government, these yielded little result and strengthened Rajapaksas’ claims that these lawsuits were examples of political victimization that would not survive judicial scrutiny. The failure of these investigations played a significant role in the return of the Rajapaksas to power in 2019.
Relations between the UNP and the SLPP changed after Sri Lanka’s economic collapse drove Gotabaya Rajapaksa from office in 2022. Wickremesinghe became president through a parliamentary vote and governed with the support of the SLPP majority. Former adversaries became partners in preserving a power structure that had benefitted both sides for decades. The alliance between the two parties validated what the Sri Lankan left had been saying for years — the established political parties are no longer distinguishable from each other and have a vested interest in preserving the status quo. This was another reason for the NPP victory in 2024.
Now in opposition, Wickremesinghe is opposing Namal’s arrest over the Airbus deal. His response is another example of how Sri Lanka’s established political elites close ranks when accountability threatens their power and privilege.
President Dissanayake recently said that Sri Lanka’s former governments had played “cops and robbers” for decades. One group pretended to pursue the other until they exchanged roles. “They were just playing a game,” he said, “but now the real police have arrived.”
Namal Rajapaksa’s arrest is important because the Airbus investigation has now crossed from investigating corporate intermediaries to the political power behind the intermediaries. It also exposes the relationship between two political camps that once pretended to be mortal enemies but now recognize a common threat in the NPP’s accountability campaign.
Sri Lanka’s previous accountability efforts failed because there was no political will on either side to punish powerful politicians.  The Yahapalanaya government’s cases against the Rajapaksas were abandoned not because they could not be proven but because the UNP and the SLPP wanted to preserve a system where former leaders were not jailed for corruption. The difference now is that the NPP has no stake in preserving the old system.
